lessons.plain: A schedule is the plan that shows which work happens when. Once a team relies on one, someone has to decide who may open and edit it, where the official copy lives, and what happens when the agreed plan must change. Those rules are schedule configuration management policies. Think of a shared family calendar: some people can only view it, one person approves new events, every earlier version is kept, and the original plan is saved so you can later see how far things drifted. Setting these rules at the start stops the schedule from becoming several conflicting copies that nobody trusts.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team's schedule lives in a shared file. Three people each keep their own edited copy, and a contractor changes a due date without telling anyone. What do you think goes wrong first, and what single rule would have prevented it?
lessons.teach:
Schedule configuration management is the set of policies that control how a schedule is accessed, stored, and changed over the life of a project. Accessibility means who may view, edit, or approve the schedule. Storage means where the single authoritative copy lives, how its version history is kept, and how it is backed up. A baseline is the approved snapshot of the schedule, with its planned dates and logic, used as the fixed reference for measuring progress. Change control is the formal process for proposing, reviewing, approving, and recording any change to that baseline.

It works because a baseline only means something if it stays fixed. If the reference point moves whenever someone edits it, nobody can tell whether the project is ahead or behind. Changes are allowed, but they must be visible and approved.

Worked example. The baseline was approved on 3 March with a finish of 30 September. In week 6 a vendor delivery slips two weeks. First, the scheduler logs a change request describing the slip and its effect on the critical path. Second, the approver named in the policy reviews the request and approves it. Third, the working schedule is updated, while the baseline keeps the original dates. Fourth, performance reports show the project two weeks behind baseline, which is the truth. Re-baselining happens only if the policy allows it and the approver signs off.

Common mistake: editing the baseline directly so the variance disappears, or letting every team member change the master file. Consequence: status reports show green while the project is actually late, and stakeholders stop trusting the schedule.

Good policy answers the who, where, and how of every change before the first change arrives.

questions.prompt: A small events company, Harbourlight Events, is setting up schedule configuration for a 14-week venue refit. Its baseline was approved on 9 June with a finish of 15 September. The team has already decided that the single authoritative schedule file lives on the company's shared project drive, that every saved revision is kept so earlier versions can be recovered, and that a copy is backed up each night to a separate off-site location. The policy list is missing one decision: the access settings that say who may edit the file, who may only view it, and who approves changes to the baseline. Which option supplies that missing decision?
choices: The baseline dates are overwritten every Friday so the file always displays current finish dates.
The nightly backup copies are deleted once the venue refit is complete to save storage space.
Each subcontractor keeps a private copy on their laptop so they can work offline, and changes are merged later by email.
The access list names who may edit, who may only view, and who approves baseline changes, and it is set before any work begins.
questions.why: Accessibility, meaning who may view, edit, or approve, is the decision the list lacks, and it has to be settled before the first change arrives.

questions.prompt: A new project's scheduler is asked what a baseline is for. Which answer is best?
choices: A copy of the schedule kept as a backup in case the main file is lost.
The latest working version of the schedule, updated daily as tasks progress.
A list of everyone who is allowed to edit the schedule file.
The approved snapshot of planned dates and logic, used as a fixed reference for measuring progress.
questions.why: A baseline is the approved snapshot of planned dates and logic that stays fixed so progress can be measured against it.

questions.prompt: On a 40-week software migration, a team lead is frustrated by a two-week slip and changes the baseline finish date back to the earlier original plan date so the dashboard stays green. Which description is most accurate?
choices: It is acceptable because the baseline is only a planning estimate and can be adjusted whenever the dashboard looks wrong.
It is a sound fix because the working schedule now matches the team's commitments.
It is fine so long as the lead records the change in a note at the bottom of the file.
It is a policy breach: the baseline should stay fixed, the slip should go through change control, and reports would then show the true variance.
questions.why: Editing the baseline to hide a variance breaks the fixed reference and bypasses the approved change process, so the reports stop reflecting reality.

questions.prompt: A design agency's schedule policy says only the project lead may approve baseline changes, all five team members may view the file, and the file sits in one shared folder with weekly archived copies. Which statement correctly classifies these decisions?
choices: All of these are storage decisions because they all concern the shared folder.
Viewing rights are a change control decision, and only the weekly archive is a storage decision.
Approval rights and weekly archives are both accessibility decisions because they control who sees the file.
Who may view and who may approve is an accessibility decision; where the single copy lives and how its archives are kept is a storage decision.
questions.why: Accessibility covers who may view, edit, or approve, while storage covers where the authoritative copy lives, its version history, and its backups.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a new teammate why we freeze the approved baseline and route schedule changes through change control instead of just updating the plan file. Name one limit or tradeoff of being this strict.
lessons.modelAnswer: The baseline is the approved reference point. It records the planned dates and logic we agreed to, so we can measure whether we are ahead or behind. If someone quietly edits the file, we lose that reference and the reports stop meaning anything. So changes go through change control: a written request states what changed and why, its impact on the critical path and budget is assessed, and an approver decides. The approved change is recorded and the version history is kept. The tradeoff is overhead. A strict process slows small corrections and can frustrate people who need to adjust daily work. The practical answer is to set thresholds in policy, so minor adjustments within available float are handled by the scheduler, while anything touching milestones or the baseline needs formal approval.
rubricPoints: The baseline is a frozen approved reference used to measure progress and variance.
Changes are proposed, assessed for impact, approved by a named authority, and recorded.
Direct edits to the baseline or master file hide real variance and destroy trust in reporting.
A named tradeoff, such as overhead or delay, with a practical mitigation like thresholds.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining why the policy exists and what it costs, which is best checked by explaining it back.

lessons.plain: Before a project builds its schedule, someone has to decide how the schedule will be planned, updated, and controlled at all. Some projects suit a detailed plan set up front. Others, where requirements shift often, suit short cycles that re-plan as they go. Choosing that style depends on what makes this particular project unusual, what the company's surroundings allow, and what the company has already learned from past work. Getting this choice right first saves a lot of rework later, because every later scheduling decision builds on it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team is building a new mobile app for a client who says they will change their mind about features every two weeks. Would you plan the whole schedule in detail on day one, or choose a different approach? Why?
lessons.teach:
A schedule approach is the overall method a project uses to build, update, and control its schedule. It covers how detailed the plan is, how often it is refreshed, how changes are approved, and how progress is reported. Project characteristics are the features that make a particular project unusual, such as its size, how uncertain the work is, whether dates are fixed by outside parties, how new the technology is, and how much change stakeholders will accept. Enterprise environmental factors, usually shortened to EEFs, are conditions outside the project team's direct control that still shape the choice, such as regulations, market conditions, company culture, and tools the company already owns. Organizational process assets, or OPAs, are what the company has already learned and stored: templates, past schedules, historical durations, policies, and lessons learned.

Why it works: the approach should match the project's real conditions. A detailed up-front plan is useful when the work is well understood and dates are fixed. Short planning cycles suit work where requirements keep moving. Using OPAs saves effort and gives better duration estimates, and checking EEFs prevents choosing a method that a regulator or a tool will not allow.

Worked example: a team installs equipment in a hospital with a fixed inspection date set by a regulator. Step 1, the characteristics: dates are fixed externally and changes are costly. Step 2, the EEFs: the regulator requires a documented baseline and formal sign-off. Step 3, the OPAs: the company has a template and durations from three similar installs. Result: a predictive approach with a detailed baseline, formal change control, and durations taken from the historical records.

Common mistake: copying the previous project's approach without asking whether its characteristics match. Consequence: a rigid baseline on a shifting software project gets broken every week, and the team spends more time explaining variances than doing the work.

The approach is decided by the project's conditions, not by habit.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm must replace its parcel sorter during a six-week shutdown window before its peak season. The control software requirements are still being negotiated with the vendor, so the scope is likely to change. Step 1, the project's characteristics: requirements are unstable, so the approach should use short planning cycles with frequent re-planning. Step 2: [missing step: the enterprise environmental factor check that the approach must pass]. Step 3, the organizational process assets: the firm's lessons-learned log shows that a previous upgrade ran three weeks late because parts arrived late, so the team uses the logged supplier lead times rather than the vendor's quoted dates.
choices: Confirm that the company's licensed scheduling tool can support rolling re-planning, since a tool that only holds one fixed baseline would block the chosen approach.
Skip any environmental check, because those checks only matter for regulated industries such as healthcare.
Copy the sorter-installation template from a 2019 project, because templates always match new conditions.
Lock a full forty-week baseline now so the vendor cannot change the scope after the schedule is approved.
questions.why: An enterprise environmental factor such as a tool the company already owns must be checked so the chosen approach is actually workable, and only the tool-support check fills that gap.

questions.prompt: A software hosting company must finish a three-month data migration before a customer contract renewal, and that renewal date cannot move. Which schedule approach best fits this project's characteristics?
choices: Plan only one week ahead and re-plan each Monday, since the team cannot predict the work anyway.
Skip the baseline entirely and track progress by asking team members how they feel about the work.
Build a detailed up-front baseline with formal change control, because the external date is fixed and changes are costly.
Use the schedule from last year's office-relocation project without checking whether its conditions match.
questions.why: A fixed external date with costly changes calls for a detailed predictive baseline with formal change control, which is the match the characteristics point to.

questions.prompt: A county agency reuses the historical task durations from a road-resurfacing project done by a crew in another region to estimate a new bridge-painting project. What is the most likely failure, and what should the team do?
choices: Organizational process assets always give exact estimates, so no adjustment is ever needed.
Historical durations from a dissimilar crew may misstate the new work, so the team should check and adjust them against its own conditions before using them.
Historical durations matter only for projects with fixed external dates, so they can be ignored here.
Using stored records means the agency never has to look at its environmental factors again.
questions.why: Organizational process assets save effort but must be checked against the new project's real conditions, since a different crew may perform differently.

questions.prompt: A nonprofit is building a volunteer-scheduling app. Which of the following is an enterprise environmental factor, as opposed to an organizational process asset?
choices: A template library of past project schedules kept by the nonprofit's operations office.
The national data-retention law the nonprofit must follow when storing volunteer records.
A lessons-learned log from the nonprofit's previous app launch.
The number of hours the lead developer worked last week.
questions.why: A legal requirement is a condition outside the team's control that shapes the approach, which is what makes it an enterprise environmental factor, while the other three are stored learning or current working data.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why you recommend a different scheduling approach for the new app than the one the company used on last year's hardware rollout. Explain to them, in your own words, how you would decide the approach, and name one limit or tradeoff of your recommendation.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing what makes this project different: the requirements are expected to change every two weeks, the client is closely involved, and the team is small. Those facts point toward a short-cycle approach, where we plan a few weeks at a time and re-check the schedule at each review. Next I would check the enterprise environmental factors, such as whether our tools and the client's contract allow short-cycle reporting, and the organizational process assets, such as the templates and lessons learned from the rollout. We would keep the rollout's approval gates only where the contract needs them. The tradeoff is that the end date becomes less certain, so the client has to accept a forecast range rather than one fixed date.
rubricPoints: Names the project characteristics that drive the approach, such as change tolerance, uncertainty, and fixed external dates.
Explains EEFs as outside conditions and OPAs as the company's own stored assets, and says both are checked.
Justifies the chosen approach by linking it to the project's characteristics rather than to habit.
States a concrete limit or tradeoff of the chosen approach.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a scheduling approach means reasoning through a situation with competing characteristics, which a scenario exercise builds better than any listed mission.

lessons.plain: Before anyone builds a project schedule, a team needs house rules for how scheduling will be done. These rules answer practical questions: which scheduling software the team will use, how small each task must be, how progress will be measured in money and time, and who has to say yes before the plan becomes official or is changed. It is like agreeing on the rules of a board game before the first move, so everyone counts points the same way. Without these rules, each person schedules differently and the numbers cannot be compared.
lessons.guessPrompt: A 25-day task is reported as 90 percent complete for four weeks in a row. What is the risk to the project, and what kind of rule would prevent it?
lessons.teach:
Scheduling policy is the written set of rules a project uses for its schedule. A procedure is the step-by-step way those rules are carried out. This objective covers four decisions. Tool selection means choosing the scheduling software and deciding what it must hold, such as the links between tasks, the resources assigned to them, and the calendars that define working days. Activity granularity means setting the maximum size of an activity, usually as a maximum duration or effort, so that progress can be checked at each reporting cycle. EVM, or earned value management, is a method that compares three figures: planned value, which is the budget for work scheduled to be done by now; earned value, which is the budget for work actually completed; and actual cost, which is what was spent. Implementing EVM means choosing how completed work is credited, for example 0/100 for short activities or a fixed percentage at milestones, and how often the figures are calculated. Approval requirements name who signs off the baseline, which is the approved version of the schedule that changes are measured against, and who must approve changes above a set threshold.

Why it works: rules decided before work starts make later numbers comparable. A variance means the same thing across teams only if everyone earned value the same way.

Worked example: a project has a 25-day activity. The policy caps activities at 10 working days and credits 0/100 for activities under 5 days. The scheduler splits the 25 days into three activities of about 8, 8 and 9 days. Each piece reports weekly. After week two, the first piece is complete and 8 days of budget is earned, so progress is visible instead of hidden at 90 percent for a month.

Common mistake: setting granularity so fine that updating the schedule takes longer than the work itself, or so coarse that progress cannot be seen at all.

Consequence: if the baseline changes without the approval the policy requires, variance reports still look normal while the plan has quietly moved, and the sponsor learns about the overrun late.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team's scheduling policy caps any activity at 6 working days and credits 0/100 for activities under 4 days. Their 14-day racking install is split into three pieces of 5, 5 and 4 days, each within the cap. A separate 3-day inspection is also in the plan. Step 1: the inspection is 3 days, which is under the 4-day threshold. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: at the end of week two the inspection is half finished, so its earned value for that week is zero. Which statement correctly fills step 2?
choices: Split the inspection into two 1.5-day pieces so that each piece can earn credit separately.
Apply the 0/100 rule, so the inspection earns its full budget only when it is complete.
Credit the inspection 50 percent at its midpoint, because short activities should show progress early.
Record planned value as earned value for the inspection so the schedule variance stays at zero.
questions.why: Under a 0/100 rule an activity under the threshold earns nothing until it is finished, which is why step 3 gives zero earned value at the midpoint.

questions.prompt: A team reports planned value of 40,000, earned value of 32,000 and actual cost of 36,000 at the end of a reporting period. Which reading is correct?
choices: The project is on schedule but over budget, because earned value equals planned value.
The project is behind schedule and over budget, because less work is complete than planned and more was spent than the work completed is worth.
The project is behind schedule only, because cost figures do not affect schedule status.
The project is ahead of schedule and under budget, because the team spent less than it planned to spend.
questions.why: Earned value below planned value means less work is done than scheduled, and actual cost above earned value means spending exceeds the budget for completed work.

questions.prompt: On a 12-person software project, the scheduling lead moves the approved baseline to absorb a two-week slip, without the sign-off the policy requires for changes of that size. Which outcome does the teaching text warn about?
choices: The change is rejected automatically by the scheduling software until the approval is recorded.
Variance reports still look normal while the plan has quietly moved, so the sponsor learns about the overrun late.
Activity granularity is reset to the default, which hides the slip in the detailed task list.
The sponsor is alerted at once, because any baseline change triggers a notice to the sponsor.
questions.why: The teaching text says that an unapproved baseline change leaves variance reports looking normal while the plan has shifted, delaying the sponsor's awareness.

questions.prompt: A team of six building a 2-month internal tool breaks its work into 300 activities of about one hour each and updates every activity in the tool weekly. What is the main risk the teaching text associates with this granularity?
choices: Stakeholders will receive too few reports because progress is hidden at the milestone level.
The tool will refuse to link tasks that are shorter than a day.
The schedule becomes so fine that keeping it updated takes longer than doing the work itself.
Earned value cannot be calculated for any activity shorter than a full week.
questions.why: The teaching text names over-fine granularity as a common mistake, where updating the schedule costs more effort than the work it tracks.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a project should write down its activity granularity and EVM rules before planning starts. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: Writing these rules down first means every planner sizes activities the same way and credits earned work the same way, so the variance numbers from different teams can be added up and compared. If we skip this, one team might report a large task as 90 percent complete for weeks, and EVM will show a healthy result right up until the deadline slips. The tradeoff is that tight granularity rules create more updating work. A policy that caps activities at 10 days means long tasks must be split, and splitting takes planning time and makes the schedule larger. So the rule should be sized to the project: small enough that progress is visible at each reporting cycle, but not so small that maintaining the schedule costs more than the work it tracks. I would also write down who approves baseline changes, so the numbers stay meaningful after the plan is set.
rubricPoints: Consistent rules let planning numbers from different teams be compared
Granularity should make progress visible at each reporting cycle
EVM needs a stated rule for crediting earned work, or results mislead
A named tradeoff, such as more updating effort from finer splits
Approval requirements keep the baseline meaningful after it is set

suggested.rationale: The core skill is justifying scheduling policy choices in your own words, which no listed mission or planned engine currently practices.

lessons.plain: Think of a schedule as one piece of a bigger plan for a project. A project management plan is the master set of approved documents that says how the project will be planned, run, and closed. The scheduling part must fit with the other parts: what the project will deliver (scope), what it can spend (cost), how good the result must be (quality), what could go wrong (risk), and what must be bought from outside (procurement). A schedule built alone will promise dates that the budget or the supplier contracts cannot support. This lesson is about making those pieces agree with each other.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team builds a detailed schedule that finishes in nine months, but the approved budget only covers seven months of staff time, and a key vendor contract ends in month six. Before reading on, what should the scheduler check, and why would the schedule alone not reveal the problem?
lessons.teach:
A project management plan is the approved set of documents that says how a project will be planned, executed, monitored, and closed. The scheduling part is one component among several. Its partners are the scope baseline (the approved description of work and what is excluded), the cost baseline (the approved spending plan over time), the quality plan (the standards deliverables must meet and how they are checked), the risk management plan and risk register (the way uncertainty is handled, and the list of identified uncertainties), and the procurement plan (what is bought from outside, when, and under which contract terms). A baseline is an approved version of a plan that later progress is measured against. Integration means making these components agree with one another and with the schedule baseline.

Why it works: each component limits the others. Scope decides how many activities exist. Cost decides how many people can work and for how long. Procurement sets external dates the schedule must respect. Risk adds reserve time and money. When one component changes, the others must be checked.

Worked example: the schedule shows nine months. Step 1: check scope. The nine-month plan includes a feature that scope excludes, so remove it, and the schedule shrinks to eight months. Step 2: check cost. The cost baseline covers seven months, so eight months leaves a funding gap. Step 3: check procurement. The vendor contract ends in month six, so the vendor-dependent work must be renegotiated or moved. Step 4: record the decision through change control and update all baselines together.

Common mistake: updating the schedule and calling the job done while the cost and procurement records stay unchanged. The schedule then looks feasible, but the budget and contracts contradict it.

In a running project, a moved date without matching procurement and cost updates books crews for work that cannot start, and the overrun only appears in month six when the money or the vendor runs out. Integrated planning is the control that prevents this.

questions.prompt: A regional food distributor is adding a route-planning system. The schedule currently shows 20 weeks. Step 1 (scope): the scope baseline excludes the driver-app export feature, but the schedule still includes it, so removing it cuts the schedule to 18 weeks. Step 2 (cost): the cost baseline funds 16 weeks of contractor time at a fixed rate, so the 18-week plan leaves a funding gap that is recorded and addressed. Step 3 is missing and must be supplied by the learner: the software licence support contract with the vendor ends at week 15, and the schedule's vendor-dependent testing runs to week 18. Which action completes Step 3 correctly?
choices: Check the quality plan only, because a change in duration does not change what deliverables must meet.
Lower the risk reserve to zero, since a shorter schedule needs less contingency.
Accept the 18-week schedule as final, since the cost check already passed and no other component depends on the schedule.
Renegotiate the vendor support term or move the vendor-dependent testing, then update the schedule, cost and procurement baselines together through change control.
questions.why: Procurement sets external dates the schedule must respect, so a vendor term ending before dependent work finishes must be resolved and all linked baselines updated together.

questions.prompt: In integrated planning, what is a baseline?
choices: The first draft of a schedule, kept for reference and never approved.
A list of every risk that has been closed during the project.
A running total of hours worked by each team member so far.
An approved version of a plan that later progress is measured against.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a baseline as an approved version of a plan that later progress is measured against.

questions.prompt: A school building project moves its roof-installation date three weeks earlier to fit a new opening deadline. Which component must be checked first because it sets external dates the schedule has to respect?
choices: The risk register, to see whether the roof has been identified as uncertain.
The quality plan, to see what standards the roof must meet.
The procurement plan, to see when the roofing materials and contractor are available under their contract terms.
The scope baseline, to see whether the roof is excluded from the work.
questions.why: Procurement covers what is bought from outside, when, and under which contract terms, and it sets external dates the schedule must respect.

questions.prompt: A team updates its schedule to finish a week sooner but leaves the cost baseline and contracts unchanged. What is the most likely consequence for the running project?
choices: The schedule looks feasible, but the budget and contracts contradict it, and the overrun appears late when money or the vendor runs out.
The quality plan is automatically rewritten to match the new dates, so no defects result.
The project finishes early with no effect on any other record, because schedule changes never affect cost.
The risk register closes every identified uncertainty, removing the chance of any later problem.
questions.why: Updating only the schedule creates a feasible-looking plan that contradicts the cost and procurement records, so the overrun surfaces only later.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who believes the scheduler's job ends once the Gantt chart is finished: how the scheduling component must fit into the broader project management plan, and name one limit or tradeoff of keeping these components aligned.
lessons.modelAnswer: The schedule is only one part of the project management plan. It has to agree with the scope baseline, cost baseline, quality plan, risk plan, and procurement plan. If I move a date, I check whether scope still matches, whether the spending plan still covers the extra months, whether vendor contracts cover the new dates, and whether the risk register needs a new reserve. Each change goes through change control so every baseline is updated together. The tradeoff is that full alignment takes time and paperwork, and every extra check slows a change down. On a small project I might use a lighter set of checks, but I still never let one baseline quietly drift away from the others.
rubricPoints: Names the other plan components (scope, cost, quality, risk, procurement) that the schedule must agree with
Explains that a change to one component requires checking the others
Describes change control or baseline updates as the mechanism that keeps them aligned
States a real limit or tradeoff, such as added time, paperwork, or slower change decisions

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises integrating planning components, so the core skill here is explaining the interdependencies in your own words.

lessons.plain: Before a project's schedule can help anyone, the people doing the work need to know three things: what the schedule is trying to achieve, who is responsible for keeping it accurate, and how changes to it get handled. This objective is about passing that information along. The scheduler is the person who builds and maintains the timeline, but they cannot do it alone. They need to explain the goals, set simple routines such as how often updates are due and who reports progress, and make sure the team understands the rules before problems appear. A schedule nobody understands is just a document nobody trusts.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team member keeps updating task dates in their own copy of the plan, and nobody else knows which copy is current. What single communication step, taken at the start of the project, would most likely have prevented this?
lessons.teach:
A scheduling objective is the measurable purpose the schedule serves, such as finishing a phase by a set date or keeping work inside a fixed window. The scheduler is the person who builds, maintains and reports on the schedule. Scheduling procedures are the agreed routines for how the schedule is updated, reviewed and changed, such as who enters progress, how often, and who approves a change to a milestone date. Communicating these to the project team means making sure every contributor knows the goals, their own part in keeping the schedule accurate, and the steps they must follow.

Why it works: a schedule is only useful if people act on the same version of it. When objectives are stated clearly, team members can judge whether a task matters to the goal. When procedures are written and shared, updates arrive on time and in a consistent form, so the scheduler can see reality rather than guessing.

Worked example: a project has a milestone to deliver a test environment by week 6. Step 1: the scheduler states the objective at kickoff, 'test environment ready by end of week 6.' Step 2: the procedure is set, so each task owner updates percent complete every Friday in the shared file. Step 3: in week 3, the database engineer reports the task is 40 percent done and warns the milestone is at risk. Step 4: because the procedure says risks to milestones go to the scheduler the same day, the scheduler re-sequences work and raises it with the sponsor in week 3, not week 6.

Common mistake: sending the schedule out once and assuming it has been understood. People change their own copies, skip updates they think do not matter, or read the objective differently from the sponsor.

Consequence: in a project with several teams, one stale copy of the schedule can make two teams build against different dates, and the conflict surfaces only at integration.

The team must hear the objectives and procedures, and confirm they understand them, before the schedule is treated as the official plan.

questions.prompt: A regional credit union is moving its loan system to a new server, with the objective 'cutover complete by end of month 4.' Step 1: the scheduler emails the objective and the update procedure to the five task owners. Step 2: the owners read the email and start work; the scheduler does not ask anyone to reply. Step 3: in month 2, the network lead's copy shows a different cutover date from the sponsor's copy, and nobody notices until the server is built. The missing step is the one that should have happened before work began, when the team confirmed the schedule was understood. Which step was missing?
choices: The scheduler should have locked the cutover date in the sponsor's copy only.
The scheduler should have sent the schedule weekly instead of once at the start.
The owners should have built their own private copies of the schedule to avoid confusion.
Each owner should have been asked to confirm back to the scheduler that they understood the objective and their update duties before the schedule was treated as official.
questions.why: The schedule should only become the official plan after the team has heard the objectives and procedures and confirmed they understand them, and the missing confirmation step is what would have caught the mismatched dates.

questions.prompt: A distribution company is adding a second warehouse, and its scheduler must write down the scheduling procedure. Which item is a procedure rather than an objective?
choices: Keeping the racking install inside a fixed two-week window.
The new warehouse is ready to receive stock by 15 March.
The scheduler is the person who builds and reports on the schedule.
Each site lead enters percent complete every Thursday, and the scheduler approves any change to the 15 March milestone.
questions.why: A procedure states the agreed routine: who enters progress, how often, and who approves a change, which is what the Thursday update and approval rule describes.

questions.prompt: At kickoff of an eight-week patient records upgrade at a hospital, the IT team asks what the scheduler's role covers. Which answer matches the scheduler's role?
choices: Does the technical work on each task while owners only report percent complete.
Builds, maintains and reports on the schedule.
Approves every individual task's hours without asking the owners.
Chooses the project budget and signs the vendor contract.
questions.why: The scheduler is the person who builds, maintains and reports on the schedule, while task owners keep their own parts accurate and the scheduler does not take over their technical work or the budget decisions.

questions.prompt: A marketing agency emails its campaign schedule to five team leads on Monday and never checks that they read it. Three weeks later, two leads are working to different launch dates. What is the most likely root cause?
choices: The team leads lacked licences for the scheduling software.
Two leads ignored the Friday update rule for their own tasks.
The agency sent the schedule once and assumed understanding, with no confirmation step, so the copies drifted apart.
The launch date was set too late in the year.
questions.why: Sending the schedule once and assuming it was understood is the common mistake that lets people work from different versions, and the absence of any confirmation step is the root cause.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never run a schedule why the scheduler must communicate objectives and procedures to the whole project team, and name one limit or tradeoff of doing this heavily, such as the time it costs or the rigidity it can create.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would tell them the schedule only works if everyone is working from the same goals and the same version of the plan. If the team does not know the milestone the schedule is protecting, they cannot tell which of their tasks is urgent, so they will guess. If the update routine is not agreed, progress arrives late or in different formats, and the scheduler ends up forecasting from stale data. So the scheduler's job includes explaining the objectives, setting the routines for updates and change requests, and confirming people understand them. The tradeoff is cost: writing procedures and holding briefings takes time away from delivery, and too many rules can make a small team slow to adapt when the plan genuinely needs to change. The procedures should be kept proportionate to the project's size and risk.
rubricPoints: Names the objectives so team members can see which work matters to the goal.
Explains the scheduler's role in building, maintaining and reporting the schedule.
States agreed procedures for updates and changes so everyone works from one version.
Names a tradeoff, such as time cost or rigidity, and suggests keeping procedures proportionate.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is telling a teammate why shared objectives and routines matter and what they cost, which is best practised by explaining it aloud.

lessons.plain: Before you can plan when work happens, you need an agreed list of what work exists. A work breakdown structure is a tree that starts with the whole project at the top and splits it into smaller pieces of deliverable, meaning the things that get produced, until each piece is small enough to estimate and hand to one person. An organizational breakdown structure is a second tree showing who or which group is responsible for the work. Where a box on the work tree meets a box on the people tree, you get a control account, a single point where one person is accountable for scope, time and cost. Think of a home renovation: rooms and tasks on one side, the trades doing the work on the other.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team of six is told to build the new reporting feature, and each person starts a different list of tasks. Without any further teaching, what single thing would you put in place before anyone starts so that the lists match and every task has one owner?
lessons.teach:
A work breakdown structure (WBS) is a hierarchy that decomposes the total scope of a project into smaller elements. Scope means everything the project must deliver. The top element is the whole project. Each level breaks a parent into children, and the bottom level holds work packages: pieces of work small enough to estimate, assign to one owner, and track. Elements are described as deliverables, things produced such as a design document or a tested module, rather than as vague actions. This keeps the tree anchored to what the project must produce.

Decomposition works because it turns a large, fuzzy promise into pieces that can each be checked. A common rule is the 100 percent rule: the children of any parent must together cover all of that parent's scope, with nothing missing and nothing added outside it.

An organizational breakdown structure (OBS) is a separate hierarchy that arranges people or groups by reporting line, showing who is responsible for which work. A control account is the management point where one WBS element meets one OBS element. It is the single place accountable for that scope, its schedule and its budget.

Worked example: a project to launch a mobile app contains the WBS element Login feature. It decomposes into Login design, Login build and Login testing. The OBS has a UX Team, which owns design, and a Mobile Team, which owns build and testing. Login design sits under the UX Team, so it becomes one control account. Login build and Login testing sit under the Mobile Team, so they form a second control account.

Common mistake: writing the WBS as a list of actions (meet client, write code) instead of deliverables, or letting several owners share one work package, which leaves nobody accountable when it slips.

Consequence: if a work package is missing from the WBS, its work is never scheduled and surfaces late as an unplanned gap.

questions.prompt: A regional food distributor is moving its cold storage to a new warehouse. Its WBS element is Temperature monitoring, which decomposes into three work packages: Sensor installation, Alert setup, and Calibration check. The OBS has a Facilities Group, which owns Sensor installation and Calibration check, and a Controls Engineering group, which owns Alert setup. Step 1 is done: the element is a deliverable, not an action. Step 2 is done: the three packages together cover all of the element's scope, with nothing missing and nothing added. Step 3 is done: each package has one OBS owner. Step 4 is still missing: state how many control accounts the Temperature monitoring element creates, and why.
choices: Two, one for each OBS owner whose group holds work packages under this element
Zero, because control accounts are only created after the schedule is baselined
Three, one for each work package, so that every package gets its own account
One, because the whole element is a single deliverable and so one account holds all of it
questions.why: A control account is the point where one WBS element meets one OBS element, and here the two OBS owners, Facilities Group and Controls Engineering, each hold part of the element, so there are two accounts.

questions.prompt: A city library is planning a renovation. Which of these is the best example of a work package in its WBS?
choices: Coordinate with the building council about the east entrance
Fabricated and installed accessibility ramp at the east entrance
Renovation of the entire library building
Make sure the project meets quality expectations
questions.why: A work package is a small deliverable that can be estimated, given one owner, and tracked, and the installed ramp is a concrete produced item, while the other options are actions, a whole-project scope, or a vague goal.

questions.prompt: A data migration parent element has three children: Extract data, Transform data, and Load data. The team later realises that Verify migrated records has no place in the tree. What is the problem, and what does it cause?
choices: Verification should be placed under Load data, which creates a circular dependency
Nothing is wrong, because verification is optional and can be done informally
The children do not cover all of the parent's scope, so verification work is never scheduled and surfaces later as an unplanned gap
The parent should be removed because it has only three children
questions.why: The 100 percent rule requires the children of a parent to cover all of its scope, and any missing work package goes unscheduled and appears late as an unplanned gap.

questions.prompt: A pump overhaul package is jointly owned by the Maintenance team and the Engineering team, with neither named as the sole owner. The package slips by two weeks. What is the main risk this creates?
choices: The OBS has too many levels, which makes the WBS deeper than it should be
The package now counts twice in the 100 percent rule, so the total scope is overstated
The package becomes a control account automatically, so the schedule updates itself
Nobody is clearly accountable for the slip, because one work package has been shared between two owners instead of one
questions.why: Each work package should have one owner, because shared ownership leaves no single party accountable when the work slips.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a WBS, an OBS and a control account relate to each other, and name one limit or tradeoff of decomposing work too finely.
lessons.modelAnswer: The WBS lists what the project must produce, broken down by deliverable until each piece is a work package someone can estimate and own. The OBS lists who or which group is responsible for that work. A control account is where a WBS element and an OBS element meet, so one named owner is accountable for that slice of scope, time and cost. The tradeoff is granularity. Decomposing too finely creates hundreds of work packages, so status reporting becomes heavy and people spend their time updating boxes instead of doing the work. Decomposing too coarsely hides risk, because a large package can slip for weeks before anyone sees it. The right level is where each package can be estimated, assigned to one owner, and checked within a normal reporting cycle.
rubricPoints: The WBS decomposes total scope into deliverable-based elements, down to work packages.
The OBS shows responsibility by person or group and is kept separate from the scope hierarchy.
A control account is the intersection of one WBS element and one OBS element, with one accountable owner.
Granularity tradeoff: decomposing too finely adds reporting overhead, while too coarse a breakdown hides slippage.

suggested.rationale: Explaining how the three structures link and where to stop decomposing is the core skill here, and no current mission practises it.

lessons.plain: A duration estimate is your best guess at how many working days a task will take. There are four common ways to make it. Analogous estimating borrows the duration of a similar past task, which is quick but rough. Parametric estimating multiplies a known rate by the amount of work, such as days per cable times the number of cables. Three-point estimating asks for an optimistic, a most likely and a pessimistic guess and combines them. PERT is a weighted version of three-point that leans toward the most likely value. The goal is not to be exactly right but to be honest about how uncertain the guess is.
lessons.guessPrompt: A task took 10 days last time, but this time it covers twice the scope. Would you write 10 days, 20 days, or something else, and why?
lessons.teach:
An activity is a piece of scheduled work with a start and a finish. Duration is the number of working periods it takes, not counting waiting time. An estimate is a judgement made with incomplete information, so it should carry a range rather than a single number.

Analogous estimating takes the actual duration of a similar past activity and adjusts it for differences in size, team or complexity. It is fast and useful early in planning, but it is only as accurate as the match between the two tasks.

Parametric estimating multiplies a unit rate by a quantity. If one cable run takes 0.5 days and there are 40 runs, the estimate is 20 days. It works only when the relationship is roughly linear and the rate has been measured, not guessed.

Three-point estimating asks for three values: optimistic (O), most likely (M) and pessimistic (P). A simple three-point average is (O + M + P) divided by 3. PERT, the Program Evaluation and Review Technique, uses a weighted average, (O + 4M + P) divided by 6, so the most likely value counts most. PERT also gives a spread, (P minus O) divided by 6, which measures how uncertain the estimate is.

Worked example: a database migration has O = 4, M = 6 and P = 14 days. Step 1: multiply M by 4 to get 24. Step 2: add O, 4 and P, 14, for a total of 42. Step 3: divide by 6 to get an expected duration of 7 days. The spread is (14 minus 4) divided by 6, about 1.7 days. A simple average would give 8 days. PERT pulls the estimate toward the likely value while keeping the long tail visible.

Common mistake: entering only the most likely value into the schedule. This treats the best realistic case as the plan and hides the risk, so milestones look safe when they are not.

Consequence in a running schedule: when several activities on the critical path are each optimistic by a few days, the finish date slips by the sum of those errors, and nobody sees it until late in the project.

questions.prompt: A council is refitting the lighting in a leisure centre pool hall. The team estimates the job with O = 3 days, M = 5 days and P = 11 days. Step 1: multiply M by 4 to get 20. Step 2 is missing. Step 3: divide the running total by 6 to get the expected duration. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Subtract O from P, giving 8, then add it to 20 for 28
Multiply O by P, giving 33, and add the 20 for 53
Average O, M and P directly: (3 + 5 + 11) divided by 3 = 6.33
Add O and P to the 20, giving 34
questions.why: PERT adds the optimistic and pessimistic values once each to the weighted most-likely term (20 + 3 + 11 = 34) before dividing by 6.

questions.prompt: A planner takes the 12-day actual duration of a similar warehouse racking installation and wants to use it for a new site that is about 25 percent smaller, with the same crew size. Which approach best fits analogous estimating?
choices: Scale for the size difference and check that crew and complexity match before relying on the figure
Keep the old 12 days, since the type of work matches
Average the 12 days with a guessed figure for safety
Scale only by crew count and ignore the site size
questions.why: Analogous estimating adjusts a past actual duration for differences in size, team and complexity, and its accuracy depends on how well the two tasks match.

questions.prompt: A transit depot installs bus-stop signs at a fixed rate of 0.75 hours per sign. There are 26 signs to install. What is the parametric estimate of the total hours?
choices: 26.75 hours
0.03 hours
34.67 hours
19.5 hours
questions.why: A parametric estimate multiplies the measured unit rate by the quantity, so 0.75 multiplied by 26 gives 19.5 hours.

questions.prompt: A team estimates a fire-door swap with O = 2 days, M = 3 days and P = 10 days. What are the PERT expected duration and spread?
choices: Expected 3.0 days, spread 8.0 days
Expected 4.0 days, spread 8.0 days
Expected 5.0 days, spread about 1.3 days
Expected 4.0 days, spread about 1.3 days
questions.why: PERT gives (2 + 4 times 3 + 10) divided by 6 = 4.0 days, and the spread is (10 minus 2) divided by 6, about 1.3 days.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose analogous estimating over PERT for an activity, and name one limit of the technique you pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would use analogous estimating early on, when a task has not been broken down and we have no measured data, but a very similar task was completed recently. We take its actual duration and adjust for differences in scope, team experience or complexity. The limit is that the estimate is only as good as the match. If the past task was done by a different team or with different tools, the number can be badly off, and it gives us no information about uncertainty. Once the work is decomposed and we can reason about best, likely and worst cases, I would switch to PERT. That gives a weighted expected duration and a spread, so the team can see which activities carry the most risk and where the schedule needs buffer. PERT still depends on the quality of the three guesses, so the estimates should come from the people doing the work.
rubricPoints: Analogous estimating borrows a similar past duration and needs a good match to be reliable
PERT uses a weighted average of optimistic, most likely and pessimistic values, with the most likely counted four times
PERT's spread shows uncertainty, which a single number hides
Each technique has a limit, such as poor analogies or unreliable three-point guesses

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers schedule estimating, so the core skill here is explaining the technique and its limits in your own words.

lessons.plain: A schedule is only useful if the order of its work is right. Sequencing means deciding which pieces of work must come before others and writing those links down as a network, so the schedule shows what can start when. A dependency is a link that says one task relies on another. A milestone is a marker for a key moment, such as a sign-off, that takes no time itself. A constraint is a fixed rule about when something may happen, such as an approval date that cannot be moved. Together these links form a model that can be recalculated whenever reality changes, which is what makes it dynamic rather than a picture drawn once.
lessons.guessPrompt: A builder must pour a concrete slab before framing walls can go on it, and an inspector must sign off the frame by a fixed date. If the pour finishes two days late, what do you expect to happen to the framing and to the sign-off date, and why?
lessons.teach:
Sequencing is the work of placing activities into a logical network in which each link is a dependency, meaning one activity relies on another. The most common dependency type is finish-to-start (FS): the successor cannot begin until its predecessor finishes. Other types are start-to-start (SS), where the successor can begin once the predecessor has begun, and finish-to-finish (FF), where the successor cannot finish until the predecessor finishes. A lag is a waiting period added to a link, such as two days of curing after concrete is poured. A milestone is a zero-duration marker for a key event. A constraint is a date rule on an activity, such as start no earlier than (SNET) or finish no later than (FNLT).

The network works because it writes down the order explicitly. When one date moves, every linked successor can be recalculated, so the model stays valid as actual progress comes in.

Worked example. Excavation takes 3 days and ends at the end of day 3. Pouring the footing (2 days) is FS after excavation, so it runs days 4 to 5. Curing is a 2-day lag after the pour, so framing (4 days, FS after the lag) starts on day 8 and ends at the end of day 11. The inspection milestone is FS after framing, so it lands at the end of day 11. The FNLT 12 constraint is met with one day of slack.

A common mistake is hard-coding a start date onto an activity that is already governed by logic. The date then overrides the links, so a slipped pour no longer moves framing and the risk stays hidden.

In a running schedule, that hidden override means the team learns about the missed sign-off only when it is too late to recover. A correctly linked model shows the consequence the day the pour slips.

The model must reflect the real order of work, and every date should be explained by a link or a stated constraint.

questions.prompt: A warehouse floor is being prepared. Epoxy coating takes 3 days and runs on days 1 to 3. A 2-day cure lag, which is a waiting period added to a link, follows the coating and covers days 4 and 5. Racking installation takes 4 days and is finish-to-start (FS), meaning it cannot begin until its predecessor, the cure, is complete. The one step left for you: state the day on which racking installation begins.
choices: Day 5
Day 8
Day 4
Day 6
questions.why: The cure is complete at the end of day 5, so racking can begin on the next day, day 6; day 4 ignores the lag, day 5 treats the lag's end as the start, and day 8 counts the lag twice.

questions.prompt: In a dependency network, what is a lag?
choices: A date rule that stops an activity from starting before a set day
A zero-duration marker for a key event
A dependency where the successor cannot finish until the predecessor finishes
A waiting period added to a link between two activities
questions.why: A lag is a waiting period placed on a link, so the successor cannot begin until the lag has passed after its predecessor.

questions.prompt: A city rooftop solar crew has its start date typed directly onto the racking task, so the task is no longer driven by its links to permit approval. The permit approval then slips by 6 days. What happens to the racking date in the model?
choices: It moves only if someone also edits the lag on the link
It stays at the typed date, so the slip stays hidden until it is too late to recover
It is removed from the network at the next recalculation
It moves automatically by 6 days, because the links still apply
questions.why: A hard-coded date overrides the links, so when the predecessor slips the successor does not recalculate and the risk stays hidden until it is too late to recover.

questions.prompt: Cable pulling for a data hall (5 days) is start-to-start (SS) with power-up (3 days), meaning cable pulling can begin once power-up has begun, with a 1-day lag added to that link. Power-up starts on day 2. On which day can cable pulling begin?
choices: Day 3
Day 2
Day 4
Day 5
questions.why: Power-up starts on day 2, and the 1-day lag on an SS link pushes the successor's start one day later, to day 3; day 2 ignores the lag, while days 4 and 5 add the lag to the wrong point or count it twice.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a schedule built from linked dependencies is more useful than a list of tasks with fixed start dates, and name one limit or tradeoff of using hard date constraints on activities.
lessons.modelAnswer: A list of fixed start dates looks neat but does not say why each task starts when it does. If one task slips, nothing tells you which later tasks are affected, so someone has to check by hand. A linked network records that framing depends on the concrete curing and the inspection depends on framing. When the pour moves, the successors move automatically, and you can see at once whether a deadline is still met. The tradeoff is that linked logic only captures what someone has modelled. Hard constraints such as a must-start date can be useful for a fixed event like a delivery, but they can also override the links and hide a real slip, so each one should be justified and reviewed.
rubricPoints: Explains that dependencies make the schedule recalculate when one date changes, while fixed dates do not
Names at least one dependency type or lag and says what it controls
States that hard constraints can override logic and hide slips, or that they are only justified for fixed external events
Notes that the network is only as accurate as the links someone has modelled

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a small set of linked activities with a deadline is the exam-style skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine covers scheduling.

lessons.plain: A project is a set of tasks, and some tasks must wait for others to finish first. The critical path is the longest chain of those linked tasks, from start to finish. Its length sets the earliest the whole project can end, so any delay on it delays the finish date. A near-critical path is a chain that almost matches that length, so a small slip could make it the new longest chain. Critical Chain, PERT and Monte Carlo simulation are four ways to find or test these routes. Think of it like finding the slowest route through a series of errands: those are the stops you cannot afford to be late for.
lessons.guessPrompt: Two chains of tasks lead to the same finish. One chain has no spare time, and the other has three days of spare time. If the first chain's task runs two days late, which chain sets the project finish date, and why?
lessons.teach:
An activity is a unit of work with a duration. A dependency is a link that says one activity cannot start until another finishes. A path is any chain of linked activities from the start to the finish. Early start and early finish are the earliest days an activity can begin and end, found by moving forward through the network (the forward pass). Late start and late finish are the latest days it can begin and end without delaying the project, found by moving backward from the finish (the backward pass). Total float, also called slack, is late finish minus early finish. An activity with zero float is on the critical path, the longest path, which has zero float throughout. A near-critical path has small but non-zero float.

Worked example. Activity A takes 3 days. B takes 2 days and follows A. C takes 5 days and also follows A. D takes 4 days and follows both B and C. Forward pass: A runs days 0 to 3. B runs 3 to 5. C runs 3 to 8. D runs 8 to 12. Backward pass from the finish at day 12: D starts at 8. C must finish by 8, so it starts at 3. B must finish by 8, so it starts at 6. A must finish by 3, so it starts at 0. Float for B is 6 minus 3, which is 3 days. Float for C is 0. The critical path is A, C, D, lasting 12 days. A, B, D is near-critical with 3 days of float.

Common mistake: picking the path with the most individual long tasks, or the one that looks busiest, instead of calculating the longest chain and its float. PERT adds three-point estimates (optimistic, most likely, pessimistic) to produce expected durations along each path. Critical Chain adds resource limits and buffers. Monte Carlo simulation samples durations many times to show how often each path turns out longest.

In a running schedule, a 2-day slip on C moves the finish by 2 days, while a 4-day slip on B moves it by 1 day, because B has 3 days of float. Near-critical paths deserve watching because they often become critical after a small change.

questions.prompt: A print shop plans a catalogue run with four activities. Design takes 4 days and has no predecessor. Quote takes 2 days and has no predecessor. Print takes 6 days and follows both Design and Quote. Bind takes 3 days and follows Print. Forward pass: Design runs days 0 to 4, Quote runs days 0 to 2, Print runs days 4 to 10, and Bind runs days 10 to 13. Backward pass from day 13: Bind starts at 10, Print starts at 4, and Design starts at 0. Quote must finish by day 4, when Print starts, so its late finish is 4 and its late start is 2. Your step: work out Quote's total float and state whether Quote is on the critical path.
choices: 0 days, on the critical path
4 days, not on the critical path
2 days, on the critical path
2 days, not on the critical path
questions.why: Total float is late finish minus early finish, which is 4 minus 2 for Quote, giving 2 days, and because it is non-zero Quote is not on the critical path.

questions.prompt: What does PERT add to a network analysis that the basic critical path calculation does not use?
choices: Random sampling of durations thousands of times
Resource limits that delay activities
A buffer placed at the project end
Expected durations from three-point estimates
questions.why: PERT uses optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic estimates for each activity to produce expected durations along each path, while the buffer, sampling, and resource limit items belong to Critical Chain or Monte Carlo methods.

questions.prompt: A greenhouse project has four activities. Prep takes 4 days and has no predecessor. Order takes 7 days and has no predecessor. Plant takes 5 days and follows both Prep and Order. Water takes 2 days and follows Plant. The longest chain is Order, Plant, Water at 14 days. Prep's chain Prep, Plant, Water totals 11 days. Which activity has the most total float?
choices: Plant
Water
Order
Prep
questions.why: Prep has the longest float at 3 days, because its chain is 3 days shorter than the 14-day critical path, while Order, Plant, and Water all have zero float.

questions.prompt: Using the same greenhouse network, where Prep has 3 days of float and the project finishes on day 14, Prep slips by 2 days. What happens to the project finish?
choices: Moves to day 13
Moves to day 16
Moves to day 15
Stays at day 14
questions.why: A slip smaller than an activity's float does not push the finish, so a 2-day slip on Prep with 3 days of float leaves the finish at day 14.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would find the critical and near-critical paths for a small set of dependent activities, and name one limit of the method you would use and what it misses.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would list each activity with its duration and its predecessors, then do a forward pass to get early start and early finish for every activity, and a backward pass from the project finish to get late start and late finish. Total float is late finish minus early finish. Activities with zero float form the critical path, and the chain with small positive float is near-critical. The main limit of this method is that it assumes fixed durations and unlimited resources. If two activities share one person, the true longest chain can be different, so the calculated critical path can be wrong. It also says nothing about how likely each path is to run long. For that you would need a range of durations, such as PERT estimates or a Monte Carlo run, and then you check how often each near-critical path becomes the longest one.
rubricPoints: Describes forward and backward passes to find early and late dates
Defines total float and links zero float to the critical path
Identifies near-critical paths as chains with small positive float
Names a limit, such as fixed durations or ignored resource conflicts
Notes that probability-based methods like PERT or Monte Carlo test how stable the path is

suggested.rationale: Critical path reasoning is best practised by working through an exam-style network where the learner must decide which chain sets the finish date, and no current mission covers this.

lessons.plain: A resource breakdown structure is a tree that sorts the people, equipment and materials a project can draw on, grouped by type and skill, the way a work breakdown structure sorts the work. Once you know what you have, you assign each activity to specific resources. A resource-constrained schedule is one whose dates respect those limits: if only one electrician exists, two jobs that need an electrician cannot run at the same time. Think of a kitchen with one oven. You cannot bake two trays at once, so the baking plan has to queue. That queue is what this objective is about.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project has three tasks that each need the same single test engineer, and the plan shows all three starting on Monday. What is wrong with that plan, and what would you change first?
lessons.teach:
A resource breakdown structure (RBS) is a hierarchy of the resources available to a project, grouped by category, such as labor by skill, equipment, and materials, with each level becoming more specific. Its purpose is to make the supply side visible, just as a work breakdown structure makes the work visible. A resource is anything an activity consumes that has a limit: a person with a skill, a machine, a license, a room. Resource assignment means linking each activity to the specific resources it needs and how many units of each. A resource calendar records the hours or days each resource is actually available, and the assignment is checked against it.

Why it works: a schedule built only from logic and durations assumes unlimited supply. Once resource limits are attached, the scheduler checks each day for over-allocation, meaning demand exceeds the units available. Resolving that conflict, usually by moving start dates, is called resource leveling. Float, also called slack, is the amount an activity can slip without moving the project finish date. Activities with float can be pushed later to remove an overload at no cost to the end date. If the conflicting activities sit on the critical path, the finish date itself moves.

Worked example: Activity A needs one tester for 3 days, Activity B needs one tester for 2 days, and both are ready on day 1. The team has one tester. Step 1: on days 1 to 3, tester demand is 2 against a supply of 1, so the day is over-allocated. Step 2: check float; B has 4 days of float. Step 3: delay B to start on day 4, so it runs days 4 to 5. Step 4: the tester now works one activity at a time. Result: B finishes on day 5 instead of day 2, and the project end date does not move.

Common mistake: assigning people by name without checking their calendars, so a person booked for full weeks who is also on leave is never flagged. Another is leveling away every overload without asking whether the delayed activity was on the critical path.

Consequence: a schedule that ignores resource limits shows a finish date the team cannot meet. The gap appears late in the project, when overtime or rework is the only remaining fix. A resource-constrained schedule shows that gap while it can still be managed.

questions.prompt: A theatre lighting crew has two electricians. Activity X (hang the rig) needs both electricians for 4 days, starting on day 1, and has 0 days of float because it sits on the critical path. Activity Y (focus the lamps) needs one electrician for 3 days, is also ready on day 1, and has 5 days of float. Step 1: on days 1 to 3, electrician demand is 3 against a supply of 2, so those days are over-allocated. Step 2: X has no float, so moving it would move the finish date, while Y has 5 days of float. Step 3 is missing: what should the team do to clear the overload?
choices: Shorten Y to one day so it no longer overlaps with X, since the overload is caused by duration.
Treat the two electricians as 1.5 people each for the overlap, so the demand of 3 counts as fitting the supply.
Delay Y so it starts on day 5, after X finishes on day 4; Y's 5 days of float absorb the change, so the end date holds.
Delay X by three days so the electricians start the rig after the lamps are focused.
questions.why: Delaying Y into its float removes the overload without moving the finish, whereas delaying X, which has no float, would push the project end date out.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines a resource breakdown structure (RBS)?
choices: A hierarchy of the resources available to a project, grouped by category and becoming more specific at each level.
A calendar that records the hours each team member is on leave during the project.
A list of work packages grouped by the deliverable they produce, used to decompose scope.
A chart of activity dependencies showing which tasks must finish before others can start.
questions.why: An RBS is a hierarchy of available resources grouped by category, which makes the supply side visible; the other options describe a WBS, a calendar, or a logic network.

questions.prompt: A scheduler has activity M needing one technician for 5 days, starting on day 1. Activity N needs one technician for 2 days, is also ready on day 1, and has 2 days of float. The team has one technician. The scheduler delays N until M finishes. By how many days does the project end date move, and what does that mean?
choices: 2 days; the float equals the delay of 2 days, so the end date is safe.
0 days; the float absorbs the delay, so the end date holds.
3 days; the delay exceeds N's float, so the end date moves unless another fix is found.
5 days; the delay equals the duration of M, so the end date moves by the full 5 days.
questions.why: N is pushed from day 1 to day 6, a 5-day slip, which exceeds its 2 days of float by 3 days, so the end date moves by 3 days unless the team adds capacity or changes the work.

questions.prompt: A planner assigns a named engineer, Priya, to 100% of three activities during week 3 without opening her resource calendar. Her calendar shows she is on leave on Thursday of that week. Which check would have caught this conflict before the schedule was published?
choices: Compare the engineer's leave and availability calendar against the dates of each assignment, since a name alone does not show when that person is free.
Count the activities per person and cap each person at five, since headcount limits capacity.
Shorten each activity's duration so the assigned work finishes before any leave period begins.
Recalculate total float across the network, because float shows when people are available to work.
questions.why: Assignments must be checked against each resource's calendar, because a person booked by name may be unavailable on specific days that a duration or float check would never reveal.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a schedule with correct dates and dependencies can still be impossible to deliver, and name what you would add to fix that, including one limit of the approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Dates and dependencies only describe the order and length of the work. They assume every activity gets the people and equipment it needs whenever it is ready. If one tester is booked for two activities that overlap, the plan shows both running at once, and the finish date is fiction. I would add a resource breakdown structure so every limited person, machine or license is listed by category, then assign each activity to specific resources with the units it needs. Next I would check each resource's calendar for over-allocation and level the schedule, moving activities with float first because that protects the end date. The limit is that leveling only shifts work within the supply we already have. If the overload sits on the critical path, the honest options are adding resources, shortening work, or accepting a later date and telling the sponsor.
rubricPoints: Explains that dependencies and durations assume unlimited resources
Names the resource breakdown structure and resource assignment with units and calendars
Describes detecting over-allocation and leveling, using float before critical-path work
States the limit: leveling cannot fix critical-path overloads, which need added supply or a later finish

suggested.rationale: An exam-style situation where one scarce resource is wanted by competing activities best builds the judgment of which activity to delay, and no listed mission or planned engine covers resource scheduling directly.

lessons.plain: An integrated master plan is a top-level outline of the major achievements a project must reach, usually written by the customer or agreed when a contract starts. Think of it as the list of checkpoints the whole effort is judged against. A statement of work describes the work the contractor must perform, and contract deadlines are the dates written into the agreement. Aligning your schedule means making sure the detailed plan you maintain actually reaches each checkpoint on or before the date the contract requires, and showing clearly where it does not. This lesson explains how to line those three things up and how to read the gaps between them.
lessons.guessPrompt: A contract says the design review must be accepted by a fixed date. Your detailed plan shows the internal design work finishing a week before that date. Is the schedule aligned with the contract? What else would you need to check before you answer?
lessons.teach:
An integrated master plan (IMP) is a hierarchy of significant events. A significant event is a named checkpoint, such as a design review, that the project uses to show progress. Each event has an accomplishment, which is the state that must be true at that point, and criteria, which are the evidence proving it is true. A statement of work (SOW) is the contract document listing the work to be done. A contract milestone is a date fixed in the agreement. The integrated master schedule (IMS) is the detailed, dated plan of activities that produces the IMP events.

Alignment means traceability. Each contract milestone should map to an IMP event, and each IMP event should map to schedule activities that feed it. Then you compare dates. Take the forecast finish of the event in your schedule, add any customer review or acceptance time, and compare the result with the contract date. The difference is either margin or a shortfall.

Worked example: the contract requires the Preliminary Design Review to be accepted by 14 March. The IMP event requires an approved design baseline document and signed interface drawings. Your schedule finishes the design work on 28 February, holds the review on 5 March, and allows five days for acceptance, giving 10 March. Margin against 14 March is four days, so the alignment holds, provided the criteria are actually in the forecast.

Common mistake: marking an event complete because a draft exists, without checking the criteria. If the document is drafted but not approved, the event has not happened, and the gap appears only when the customer rejects the deliverable and downstream work stalls.

A schedule that reaches a milestone on paper but does not satisfy the IMP criteria is not aligned, and the gap must be reported as a risk rather than hidden.

questions.prompt: A ground-software team has a contract milestone requiring its Factory Acceptance Test report to be accepted by 22 May. The IMP event 'Test Readiness' is accomplished when test procedures are signed and the test environment is baselined, and its criteria are signed procedures plus a completed environment checklist. Trace it: Step 1: the event maps to two schedule activities, 'Write test procedures' (finishes 2 May) and 'Baseline test environment' (finishes 9 May). Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: the forecast acceptance date is 19 May, which leaves a margin of three days before 22 May. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Treat Test Readiness as complete on 2 May because the procedures exist as drafts
Move the contract milestone to 19 May so the margin reads zero
Compare the 9 May environment baseline directly with 22 May and skip the review
Hold the readiness review on 12 May and add the seven-day customer acceptance time to reach the forecast date
questions.why: The forecast must include the readiness review date plus the customer acceptance time, since the event only counts once it is accepted and its criteria are met.

questions.prompt: A bridge project has an IMP event called 'Load Test Plan Ready.' Which statement describes its criteria, meaning the evidence that proves the event has happened, rather than its accomplishment, meaning the state that must be true?
choices: The contract milestone date of 1 June
The load test plan is in a state where a tester could run it without further changes
A signed load test plan and a sign-off record from the independent reviewer
