The bridge is open to traffic before the load test begins
questions.why: Criteria are the evidence, such as a signed plan and a reviewer's record, while the accomplishment is the state the plan must reach.

questions.prompt: A ground-equipment contract sets a milestone of 30 September. The schedule forecasts the event finishing 15 September, and the customer needs 12 calendar days to accept the deliverable. What is the margin or shortfall against the contract date?
choices: 3 days of margin
15 days of margin
12 days of margin
A 3-day shortfall
questions.why: Adding 12 days to 15 September gives 27 September, which is three days before 30 September, so the margin is three days.

questions.prompt: A team's interface drawing is unsigned, but its schedule shows the 'Interface Definition' event as complete because the design work is finished. What should the project manager do?
choices: Mark the event complete, since the design work is finished and the schedule shows it done
Wait for the customer to reject the drawing before reporting a gap
Remove the event from the IMP so the alignment check passes
Report the event as at risk and show the unsigned drawing as an unmet criterion
questions.why: An event whose criteria are not met is not aligned, so the gap must be reported as a risk rather than hidden behind a finished-looking schedule.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would check that the detailed schedule supports a contract milestone. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start from the contract date and trace back. I find the IMP event that the milestone corresponds to, and I read its accomplishment and criteria so I know what evidence proves it is done. Then I follow the schedule activities that feed that event and take their forecast finish, adding any customer review or acceptance time. The difference between that date and the contract date tells me whether we have margin or a shortfall. The main limit is that this check is only as good as the forecast. If durations are optimistic or the acceptance time is guessed, the margin looks better than it is. So I report the margin with its assumptions, and I flag the milestone as a risk when the margin is thin, rather than presenting a single confident date.
rubricPoints: Trace each contract milestone to an IMP event and its criteria
Compare the forecast finish, including review or acceptance time, with the contract date
Report the difference as margin or shortfall
Name a limit, such as reliance on the accuracy of forecast durations

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a contract milestone against an IMP event and a forecast date is an exam-style situation that adds more than a listed mission would, and no current mission or planned engine covers it directly.

lessons.plain: Schedule risk analysis asks how likely a project's target dates are to hold, given that task lengths are only estimates. Instead of trusting one finish date, you test the plan against many possible outcomes. A what-if check changes one assumption, such as a delivery arriving late, and shows what moves. Monte Carlo simulation runs this test at scale: a computer picks random task lengths within each estimated range, recalculates the finish, and repeats this thousands of times. The result gives the chance of meeting a deadline, which you compare with how much risk the sponsor will accept. It is like checking whether you will reach an airport on time by simulating traffic many times rather than assuming the best-case drive.
lessons.guessPrompt: A plan shows a milestone finishing on day 55 against a day 60 deadline, and three of its tasks have wide uncertainty. Do you feel confident the milestone will be met, and what would you check before saying so?
lessons.teach: Schedule risk analysis tests a plan against uncertainty instead of trusting one date. A single-point schedule uses one duration per activity, usually the most likely value, and produces one finish date. Real durations vary, so that date is only one possible outcome. Schedule risk analysis asks how likely a milestone is to be met. A what-if scenario changes one assumption, such as a vendor arriving two weeks late, and recalculates the finish to see the impact. Monte Carlo simulation goes further. Each uncertain duration is given a low, most likely, and high estimate, which is a three-point range. For every run, the computer draws a random value from each range, recalculates the network, and repeats this thousands of times. The results form a distribution of finish dates. Risk tolerance is the confidence level the sponsor accepts, for example that the milestone must be met with 80 percent confidence, often called P80. Worked example: a milestone is due on day 60. Three activities run in sequence: design (15, 20, 30 days), build (20, 25, 40) and test (8, 10, 16). Using most-likely values gives 55 days, which looks safe. Averaging each three-point range gives about 61 days, already past the deadline. Across simulated runs, roughly 4 in 10 finish by day 60. To reach 80 percent confidence the finish must sit near day 66, so the team needs about six days of buffer or a change that narrows the build range. A what-if run that lowers the build high estimate from 40 to 32 shows how much that single fix helps. Common mistake: presenting the most-likely date as the commitment, which gives the milestone roughly even odds of slipping at best. Consequence: a milestone tied to a contract date and committed at 50 percent confidence will probably be missed, triggering change requests and penalties. A milestone is only achievable within risk tolerance when its simulated probability meets the agreed confidence level.

questions.prompt: A warehouse system cutover must be live by day 45. Three activities run one after another, each with a low, most likely, and high estimate in days: data cleanse (10, 12, 18), interface build (14, 18, 26), and cutover rehearsal (5, 6, 9). Step 1: the most-likely durations sum to 36 days. Step 2: a Monte Carlo run of 5,000 simulations shows the 80th-percentile finish at day 49. Step 3: the sponsor's risk tolerance is 80 percent confidence, and the milestone is day 45. Which conclusion completes the analysis?
choices: The milestone is achievable at 50 percent confidence because the middle of the distribution is near day 45.
The milestone is achievable because the most-likely total of 36 days is under the deadline of 45 days.
The milestone is not achievable, so the team should commit to day 49 as the new deadline and drop the sponsor's confidence requirement.
The milestone is not achievable within risk tolerance, so the team needs about four days of buffer or a narrower range, which a what-if run can test.
questions.why: A milestone is achievable within risk tolerance only when its simulated probability meets the agreed confidence level, and day 49 at 80 percent confidence exceeds the day 45 deadline by four days.

questions.prompt: In schedule risk analysis, what does a what-if scenario do?
choices: It draws random durations from every three-point range and recalculates the network thousands of times.
It averages all low, most likely, and high estimates into one duration for each activity before scheduling.
It replaces the sponsor's risk tolerance with the most-likely finish date so the commitment is simpler.
It changes one assumption, such as a supplier arriving late, and recalculates the finish date to show that change's impact.
questions.why: A what-if scenario isolates one changed assumption and recalculates the finish to measure its effect, which is different from the random sampling used in Monte Carlo simulation.

questions.prompt: A team has a single-point plan that finishes on day 38 for a milestone due on day 40. The sponsor requires 90 percent confidence. A simulation shows the milestone is met in 84 percent of runs. What is the correct judgment?
choices: The milestone is within tolerance because 84 percent is close to 90 percent.
The milestone can be committed at the single-point date because simulations only matter when the plan is late.
The milestone is not within tolerance, because 84 percent falls short of the agreed 90 percent confidence.
The milestone is safe because the single-point finish is two days early.
questions.why: Achievability depends on whether the simulated probability meets the agreed confidence level, and the single-point date is only one possible outcome, so the two-day margin does not prove the milestone.

questions.prompt: Why does Monte Carlo simulation produce a distribution of finish dates rather than one date?
choices: Because each uncertain activity has a three-point range, and every run draws a random value from each range before recalculating the network, so the many runs spread the possible finishes out.
Because the most-likely value is always replaced by the high estimate, which pushes every run later.
Because the software rounds each activity to the nearest week, which creates a spread of finish dates.
Because the sponsor chooses a different milestone date for each run to test their tolerance.
questions.why: Monte Carlo simulation repeatedly samples each three-point range and recalculates the network, so the set of resulting finish dates forms a distribution rather than a single outcome.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a schedule that shows a milestone on time using most-likely durations can still be unsafe to commit to, and name one limit of the Monte Carlo result you would mention.
lessons.modelAnswer: A most-likely schedule gives one finish date, but every duration is an estimate, and the finish only lands on that date if everything goes at its typical pace. Tasks in a chain tend to run longer than their most-likely value when their upper estimates are wide, so the simulated average finish is often later than the single-point date. Monte Carlo simulation handles this by drawing random durations from each three-point range and recalculating the finish thousands of times, which gives the probability of meeting the milestone. We then compare that probability with the confidence level the sponsor accepts, such as 80 percent. One limit to mention is that the result is only as good as the ranges we feed in. If the low, most likely, and high estimates are optimistic, or if we miss a risk that is not in the model at all, the probability looks better than reality. So the simulation should be paired with a review of the assumptions.
rubricPoints: Single-point most-likely schedules hide the spread of possible finish dates.
Monte Carlo draws durations from ranges and recalculates many times to give a probability of meeting the milestone.
The probability is compared against the sponsor's risk tolerance or confidence level.
The result depends on input ranges and on risks not modelled, so assumptions need review.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers schedule risk analysis, so reasoning through an exam-style milestone scenario with what-if and simulation results adds the most.

lessons.plain: When a team agrees on a schedule, the agreed version becomes the baseline: a saved snapshot that everyone accepts as the yardstick for judging progress. Getting stakeholder consensus means the people who fund, use, or are affected by the work review that plan and agree to it, so nobody can later say they never accepted those dates. The Performance Measurement Baseline (PMB) is the combined yardstick of scope, schedule, and cost, spread over time so you know how much work and money should be finished by any given date. It works like agreeing on the race distance and target split times before the start, so you can later tell whether you are ahead or behind.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a project manager updates the schedule every week to match what actually happened, what happens to the team's ability to tell whether the project is late?
lessons.teach:
A baseline is the approved version of a plan that you freeze and compare against. Stakeholder consensus is the agreement of the people with a stake in the work (sponsors, customers, functional leads, anyone whose time or money is involved) that the baseline is realistic and that changes to it will go through a formal change process. The Performance Measurement Baseline, or PMB, is the time-phased total of planned work and budget for the scope in the baseline, usually including the schedule and cost baselines together. Its main job is to give a fixed plan value for each date, so later progress can be measured against it.

The idea works because progress only means something against a fixed reference. If the plan moves every week, a late project looks on track.

Worked example: a rollout has an approved PMB of 120,000 spread evenly over 12 weeks, so 10,000 of work is planned per week. At week 6 the planned value (PV) is 60,000. The team has finished work the plan valued at 45,000, which is the earned value (EV). The schedule variance is EV minus PV, which is 45,000 minus 60,000, or negative 15,000. The project is behind, and the number is meaningful only because the 60,000 comes from a frozen baseline.

Common mistake: re-baselining whenever dates slip, which hides the slip. Re-baselining is allowed only through an approved change with stakeholder sign-off, with the old baseline kept on record.

In a running system, a frozen PMB lets a sponsor see drift early and decide whether to add resources, cut scope, or accept a later date.

questions.prompt: A software team has an approved baseline of 96,000 spread evenly over 8 weeks, so 12,000 of work is planned per week. At the end of week 5 the team has earned 72,000 of value. Step 1: the planned value at week 5 is 5 times 12,000, which is 60,000. Step 2: the earned value is 72,000. Step 3 is left for you: compute the schedule variance from these two numbers and state what it tells the sponsor.
choices: SV equals PV minus EV, which is 60,000 minus 72,000, or negative 12,000, so the project is behind plan.
SV equals EV minus PV, which is 72,000 minus 60,000, or positive 12,000, so the project is ahead of the frozen plan.
The team should re-baseline to 72,000 so that the variance reads zero and the report looks clean.
Variance cannot be computed for this team because the baseline has not yet been signed by the functional leads.
questions.why: Schedule variance is earned value minus planned value taken from the frozen baseline, so 72,000 minus 60,000 gives positive 12,000, meaning ahead of plan.

questions.prompt: A logistics company is planning a nine-month warehouse fit-out. Which statement best describes its Performance Measurement Baseline?
choices: The written record that stakeholders have agreed the plan is realistic, signed before any work starts.
The actual cost incurred to date, compared against the original estimate at each progress review.
The full list of activities and durations, kept as the working plan that the team edits every day.
The time-phased total of planned work and budget for the baselined scope, giving a fixed planned value for each date.
questions.why: The PMB is the time-phased combination of planned work and budget for the baselined scope, which gives a fixed planned value for each date; the other options describe a working schedule, a consensus record, or actual cost.

questions.prompt: A clinic software project slips two weeks in month three. The project manager quietly moves the baseline dates forward to match the new forecast and reports the project as on track. What is the main problem with this?
choices: Nothing is wrong, because baselines are meant to be updated to match the latest forecast each month.
The fixed reference is lost, so the slip is hidden and later variance can no longer show drift against the original approved plan.
Project managers have no right to report progress at all until the project is closed out.
The planned values for earlier months become too high, so the cost estimate must be doubled.
questions.why: Moving the baseline without an approved change removes the fixed reference, so the slip disappears from the measurements instead of being visible against the approved plan.

questions.prompt: A construction firm is building a 14-month office block. The sponsor, the customer, and the electrical lead all have a stake in the schedule. What does obtaining stakeholder consensus on the baseline require?
choices: The sponsor, the customer, and the functional leads agree the baseline is realistic and that later changes need formal approval.
Only the scheduler signs the baseline, because the scheduler owns the network diagram.
Each stakeholder keeps a personal copy of the plan and updates it as their own needs change.
Consensus is reached as soon as the material supplier accepts the purchase price, regardless of internal leads.
questions.why: Consensus means the people with a stake in the work agree the baseline is realistic and that changes will go through a formal change process, which is the only option that describes both parts.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why the project needs an approved, frozen baseline and PMB before it reports progress, and name one limit or tradeoff of freezing the plan.
lessons.modelAnswer: We agree the baseline with stakeholders first so every later progress report is measured against the same plan that people accepted. The PMB adds the budget to the schedule, so for any date we know how much work and cost should be done, and we can calculate whether we are ahead or behind. Without a frozen version, each weekly update quietly moves the target, and lateness disappears. The tradeoff is rigidity: a frozen plan can be wrong about things we only learned later, so we need a formal change process to revise it. Each change needs stakeholder approval and the old baseline stays on record. Freezing gives honest measurement, but it costs some flexibility and a lot of discipline about how changes get approved.
rubricPoints: Explains that the approved baseline is a fixed reference for measuring progress
Describes the PMB as schedule and cost combined over time, giving planned value by date
Notes that stakeholder consensus and sign-off make the plan accountable
Names a tradeoff, such as rigidity or the need for a formal change process

suggested.rationale: Explaining why a frozen baseline matters and what it costs is the core skill here, and no listed mission covers stakeholder sign-off.

lessons.plain: Schedule status collection means regularly gathering facts about what work has actually happened: which tasks started, which finished, how much is done, and how much is left. You collect these facts at set times, such as every Friday, by asking people in reports, meetings, and on-site checks. Then you enter those facts into the schedule so it reflects reality instead of the plan. Without this, the schedule keeps describing the world as it was supposed to be, and every later decision rests on out-of-date information. Think of it as taking a regular reading from the gauges before deciding where to steer.
lessons.guessPrompt: A task was planned to take five days and has been running for three days. Two people tell you it is about half done, but one says it is nearly finished. Before reading anything else, what would you check before you change the schedule, and why?
lessons.teach:
Key terms. The schedule model is the working file that holds every activity, its duration, its dependencies, and its dates. The baseline is a saved copy of the approved plan, kept as the yardstick for comparison. The status date, also called the data date, is the cut-off moment up to which the schedule reflects actual progress; anything after it is still forecast. Remaining duration is how much work is still left on an activity. It is separate from percent complete, because a task can be half done by effort and still have most of its time ahead.

Why it works. A schedule is only a forecast until actuals are entered. Each status cycle gives the model new facts: actual start, actual finish, and remaining duration. The scheduling engine then recalculates forecast finish dates for successor work and the critical path. Collecting at a fixed interval keeps cycles comparable. Combining three channels helps: reports supply numbers, meetings surface blockers and assumptions, and inspections confirm physical progress rather than opinion.

Worked example. Pour foundation was baselined at five days starting Monday, with a status date of Wednesday end of day. The site inspection on Wednesday shows the concrete poured and curing on two of the five planned days of work, and the crew lead agrees. Step 1: record the actual start as Monday. Step 2: set remaining duration to three days, not two, because the inspection found the forms need rework. Step 3: set percent complete to about 40 percent, derived from the inspection rather than the crew's estimate. The engine now pushes the finish of successor tasks out by one day.

Common mistake. Teams copy the reported percent complete straight into the model and never reset remaining duration. A task reported as 90 percent complete for three weeks looks almost finished, so the forecast finish stays too early and the critical path is misread.

Consequence. Inflated progress hides slippage until late in the project, when the lost float is gone and recovery options are expensive and limited.

questions.prompt: A warehouse crew is installing storage racking in aisle 4. The baseline planned 8 working days for this installation. The crew started on Tuesday, and at the Thursday status date (end of day) an inspection confirms racking is fully installed on 3 of the 8 planned days of work, with no rework needed. Step 1: record the actual start as Tuesday. Step 2: record percent complete as about 37 percent, derived from the inspection. Step 3: set remaining duration, which is how much work is still left on the activity, to what value?
choices: 3 days, the work already completed
8 days, the original baseline duration
5 days, the planned 8 days minus the 3 days the inspection confirms as done
6 days, the planned 8 days minus the 2 days between Tuesday and Thursday
questions.why: Remaining duration is the planned length minus the work the inspection confirms as finished, and with no rework found that leaves 5 days.

questions.prompt: A cutover team sets its status date to Friday at 5 pm. On Monday, a report arrives saying a task finished on Saturday at 9 am. How should this completion be handled in the status cycle that uses the Friday status date?
choices: Leave the task as forecast, because the status date is the cut-off and anything after it is not yet actual progress
Record the finish as Friday at 5 pm so the cycle stays tidy
Delete the task's remaining duration so the scheduling engine ignores it
Record Saturday at 9 am as the actual finish, since it is the most recent information available
questions.why: The status date is the cut-off up to which the schedule reflects actual progress, so a Saturday event belongs to a later cycle and remains forecast for now.

questions.prompt: A 10-day task started on schedule. At day 7, the report says it is 90 percent complete, but the remaining duration field still holds the 1 day it was set to at an earlier cycle. An inspection shows about 3 days of work actually remain. What is the most likely effect on successor tasks in the schedule model?
choices: No effect, because the engine uses percent complete alone to calculate finish dates
The engine flags a negative float automatically, so the error is caught without review
Successor forecast dates come out too early, because the model believes only one day of work remains
Successor forecast dates come out too late, because percent complete above 50 pushes them out
questions.why: Copying percent complete without resetting remaining duration leaves the model thinking little work is left, so successor and critical path dates are forecast too early.

questions.prompt: At a weekly meeting, a mechanical contractor says the chiller pad is ready. A site walk afterward shows the anchor bolts are not yet set. Which information channel most directly corrects this for the schedule model, and why?
choices: The monthly cost report, because financial data is the most reliable source of progress
The meeting minutes, because the discussion is where the assumption was first recorded
A physical inspection, because it confirms what has actually been built rather than what people believe
The team's verbal agreement in the meeting, because the people present all agreed
questions.why: Inspections are the channel that confirms physical progress rather than opinion, so the unset bolts should be reflected through an inspection finding.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how and when you collect activity status for the schedule, and name one limit of relying on status reports alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: I collect status on a fixed rhythm, say every Friday at a set cut-off, so every update is comparable. I pull three kinds of input: written reports from task owners, a short status meeting where blockers and assumptions come up, and field inspections where someone checks physical progress. Then I update the schedule model: actual starts and finishes, remaining duration for work in progress, and percent complete tied to what was observed. The engine then recalculates the forecast finish and the critical path. The limit I would flag is that self-reported status is optimistic and often rounds up, so reports alone can hide slippage. That is why I verify high-risk or long-running activities by inspection before accepting the numbers, and why I reset remaining duration instead of just bumping the percentage.
rubricPoints: Collection happens at defined intervals against a fixed status date or cut-off.
Sources include reports, meetings, and inspections, each used for a different kind of fact.
The model is updated with actual dates, remaining duration, and verified percent complete, then recalculated.
Names a limit such as optimistic self-reporting and the need to verify high-risk activities.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers schedule status collection, so reading the teaching text is the best fit.

lessons.plain: Schedule analysis means reading a project's timeline against what has actually happened, then working out what it means: which tasks are slipping, whether the finish date is at risk, what caused it, and who needs to know. It is like checking a road-trip map against the odometer and fuel gauge at a stop. You are not only noting that you are behind. You are asking whether you will still reach the destination, which stretch is causing the delay, and what decision the driver needs to make next. A good analysis ends in a report that states the status, the change, the impact on the finish, and the open issues, so someone can act on it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project's baseline finish is day 40. Task A is on the chain of dependent tasks that sets the finish, and it is 3 days late with no spare time. Task B is 2 days late but has 4 days of spare time before it could delay anything. Which one do you report first as the bigger threat to the finish date, and why?
lessons.teach:
A schedule analysis compares the current schedule with the baseline, which is the approved plan of dates and work that progress is measured against. Schedule variance is the gap between a task's planned dates and its actual or forecast dates. The critical path is the longest chain of dependent tasks from start to finish; any delay on it moves the project end date. Total float (also called slack) is how many days a task can slip before it pushes the end date. Critical-path tasks have zero float. The forecast finish is the end date you expect if current progress continues, and the impact is the difference between that forecast and the baseline finish.

Why it works: a late task only matters to the end date in proportion to the float it uses up. A raw count of late tasks hides this, so the analysis asks two questions for each variance: how much float is left, and is this task on the path that sets the finish?

Worked example: the baseline finish is day 40. Task A has zero float and is 3 days late, so the forecast finish moves to day 43, an impact of 3 days. Task B is 2 days late but has 4 days of float. Its slip uses 2 of those days, the forecast finish stays at day 40, and only 2 days of float remain for B. Report A as a finish-date threat and B as a float warning.

Common mistake: reporting percent complete or the number of late tasks as the project status. The consequence is that the team spends effort on B while A quietly sets the finish. When B later runs out of float it becomes critical too, and two paths compete for the same people and resources.

An analysis is complete only when each finding is stated as status, change, impact, and open issue.

questions.prompt: A hospital pharmacy fit-out has a baseline finish of day 75. Total float (the number of days a task can slip before it pushes the end date) is the measure used here. Task N has 6 days of float and is 4 days late. Step 1: N has 6 days of float. Step 2: the 4-day slip uses 4 of those days, so the forecast finish stays at day 75. Step 3 is missing. Which choice correctly completes step 3?
choices: 2 days of float remain for N, so report N as a finish-date threat because it is 4 days late
2 days of float remain for N, so report N as a float warning rather than a finish-date threat
6 days of float remain for N, because float only changes once the task is complete
0 days of float remain for N, so N is now critical and the finish moves to day 79
questions.why: Subtracting the 4-day slip from the 6 days of float leaves 2 days, and because the forecast finish has not moved, the right report is a float warning rather than a finish-date threat.

questions.prompt: A clinic's baseline finish is day 52. Task X is on the critical path (zero float) and is 2 days late. Task Y has 5 days of float and is 3 days late. Using the forecast finish and the impact (the difference between the forecast finish and the baseline finish), which statement is correct?
choices: Forecast finish is day 54 and the impact is 2 days; X is the finish-date threat and Y is a float warning with 2 days remaining
Forecast finish is day 57 and the impact is 5 days; both tasks must be reported as finish-date threats
Forecast finish is day 55 and the impact is 3 days; Y is the finish-date threat
Forecast finish is day 52 and the impact is 0 days; X is only a float warning
questions.why: X has zero float, so its 2-day slip moves the forecast finish from day 52 to day 54, while Y's 3-day slip uses only part of its 5 days of float and leaves 2 days, so it does not move the finish.

questions.prompt: A status report for a school building project says 9 of 14 tasks are late and 70 percent of the work is complete, and it concludes the finish date is at risk. What is the best next step under a correct schedule analysis?
choices: Ask the team to work overtime on every late task until the count of late tasks falls
For each late task, check how much float is left and whether it lies on the critical path, then determine its effect on the forecast finish
Re-sequence all late tasks in order of how many days late they are
Report the 70 percent complete figure to the sponsor, since it summarises overall status
questions.why: A raw count of late tasks or percent complete hides which variances move the end date, so each variance must be tested against remaining float and the critical path before the finish impact is judged.

questions.prompt: A warehouse fit-out analysis has found that a conveyor install task is 3 days behind its planned dates. Which of the following is a complete finding under a proper schedule analysis?
choices: The conveyor task is behind, so the team should watch it closely next week

Status: conveyor install is 3 days late against baseline. Change: its forecast dates have moved by 3 days. Impact: 0 days on the finish if float covers it, otherwise the forecast finish moves. Open issue: how much float remains and whether the task is on the critical path
The conveyor task is 3 days late and has a lot of work left
The conveyor task is 3 days late, so the project will be late by 3 days
questions.why: A complete finding names the status, the change, the impact on the end date, and the open issue still to resolve, which is the only choice that covers all four parts without assuming the impact before checking float.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would turn a list of late tasks into a status report for the sponsor. Name one limit of the method you use.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not start from the late-task list. I would check each late task against the baseline and its remaining total float, then trace which chain of dependent tasks sets the forecast finish date, which is the critical path. Each finding gets four lines: the status (what slipped and by how much), the change (what moved since the baseline), the impact (the effect on the finish date in days, measured against the baseline finish), and the open issue (what decision or fix is needed, and who owns it). The limit is that the forecast depends on current remaining-duration estimates, which are often optimistic. So I would state those assumptions beside the forecast and say which estimates are least certain, so the sponsor does not read the date as firmer than it is.
rubricPoints: Starts from the baseline and the critical path, not from a count of late tasks
Uses total float to separate tasks that threaten the finish from tasks that only consume spare time
Reports each finding as status, change, impact on the finish date, and open issue
Names a real limit, such as dependence on uncertain remaining-duration estimates

suggested.rationale: Deciding which slip threatens the finish date is best practised through exam-style situations with dates and float to reason through, and no listed mission or planned engine covers schedule analysis.

lessons.plain: What-if scenario analysis means asking 'what happens to the finish date if we change how the work is done?' before changing anything real. You copy the schedule, change one or more assumptions such as overlapping two tasks, adding people to a slow task, or changing the order, and then recalculate to see the new end date, the cost, and the risk. You compare the options side by side and pick the one that best meets the goal. The original approved plan stays untouched until someone with authority approves a change.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project is due in 25 days, but the current plan finishes in 27 days, and the critical task is a 10-day testing step. Before reading on, name two different ways you could shorten the finish date, and give one reason you would not simply pick whichever option shortens it the most.
lessons.teach:
The schedule model is the working set of activities, their durations, and the dependencies between them (links that say which task must wait for which). The critical path is the longest chain of dependent activities; it sets the earliest finish date, so any delay on it moves the project end. Float is how far an activity can slip without moving that end date. A what-if scenario is a test run on a copy of the model, in which you change one or more assumptions and recalculate.

Why it works: recalculating shows effects that are hard to predict by hand. Changing one link can shift the critical path onto a different chain, so the option that looks best at first is often not the best after recalculation. Two common options are fast tracking, which overlaps two dependent activities planned in sequence (it saves time but adds rework risk), and crashing, which adds resources to a critical activity to shorten it (it usually adds cost).

Worked example. The model shows Build at 15 days, then Test at 10 days, then Release at 2 days, for a finish on day 27 against a deadline of day 25. Option A: start Test after 5 days of Build, overlapping 5 days. The chain shortens to 22 days, plus an expected 2 days of rework, giving day 24. Option B: add a second tester so Test takes 6 days, giving day 23 at extra cost. For each copy, recalculate, then record finish date, cost, and risk before comparing.

Common mistake: running the experiment on the approved baseline and overwriting it, or choosing the earliest date while ignoring cost and risk.

Consequence: if the chosen option changes the approved plan, it must pass through formal change control, and the baseline is updated only through that process. Otherwise, performance reports compare work against a plan nobody approved.

questions.prompt: A cold-storage warehouse fit-out at Northgate Logistics has this schedule model: Insulate walls takes 9 days, then Install racking takes 10 days, then Commission cooling takes 2 days, for a finish on day 21 against a deadline of day 18. The team runs a what-if option that starts racking after 6 days of insulation, overlapping 3 days, which shortens the chain by 3 days to 18 days. Step 1 (done): the recalculated chain is 18 days before rework. Step 2 (done): the overlap carries an expected 2 days of rework. Step 3 (you do this): add the expected rework to the shortened chain to get the realistic finish day. What is that realistic finish day?
choices: Day 21
Day 23
Day 18
Day 20
questions.why: Adding the 2 expected rework days to the recalculated 18-day chain gives day 20, whereas day 18 ignores the rework, day 21 is the original unchanged finish, and day 23 counts the rework twice.

questions.prompt: An activity has 4 days of float (the amount it can slip without moving the project end date). It slips 3 days. What happens to the project end date?
choices: It holds, because the 3-day slip is within the 4 days of float
It moves by 3 days, because any slip on any activity moves the end
It holds, because float only matters for activities already on the critical path
It moves by 1 day, because float is subtracted from the slip before the end is set
questions.why: Float is the slack an activity can absorb without moving the end date, so a 3-day slip against 4 days of float leaves the end date unchanged.

questions.prompt: A scheduler tests a compressed repair plan by changing durations directly in the approved baseline file, decides the option is not worth it, and leaves the changed durations in place. What is the main problem?
choices: The test was run too quickly to be reliable
The approved plan is now altered without change control, so later performance reports compare work against a plan nobody approved
The critical path cannot be recalculated once a baseline exists
Only fast tracking is permitted on a baseline, so the crash changes were invalid
questions.why: A what-if run must happen on a copy, because the baseline may change only through formal change control, and overwriting it makes later reports compare work against an unapproved plan.

questions.prompt: On a copy of a schedule with a deadline of day 26, three what-if runs produce these results. Run 1 adds resources to a critical task, finishing on day 24 at an extra cost of 18,000. Run 2 overlaps two dependent tasks, finishing on day 25 at no added cost but carrying an expected 3 days of rework. Run 3 changes nothing and finishes on day 27. Which conclusion best follows?
choices: Run 3 should be chosen because it leaves the approved plan untouched and so carries no risk
Run 1 should be rejected because adding resources never shortens a critical task enough to meet a deadline
Run 2 misses day 26 once expected rework is added, so Run 1 is the only option that meets the deadline, at 18,000 extra cost, and it must go through change control
Run 2 is the best choice because it finishes earliest once no added cost is counted
questions.why: Run 2's 25 days plus 3 rework days gives day 28, which misses the deadline, so Run 1 is the only run that meets day 26, and its cost means it must pass through formal change control before it changes the approved plan.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what what-if scenario analysis is for in schedule control, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: What-if scenario analysis lets us test options on a copy of the schedule before committing to one. We change an assumption, such as overlapping two dependent tasks or adding people to a critical task, recalculate, and compare the new finish date with the cost and risk each option adds. It is useful because the critical path can move when we change a link, so the obvious fix is not always the best one. The limit is that results are only as good as the estimates we feed in. Fast tracking in particular looks cheap on the schedule but can hide rework that the model does not show. So the chosen option needs a risk check, and if it changes the approved plan, it goes through formal change control rather than being copied straight into the baseline.
rubricPoints: Describes what-if analysis as recalculating alternatives on a copy of the schedule model, without changing the approved baseline.
Explains that changing dependencies or resources can move the critical path, so results must be compared, not assumed.
Names a limit or tradeoff, such as added rework risk from fast tracking or added cost from crashing.
States that an option adopted into the approved plan goes through formal change control and a baseline update.

suggested.rationale: A deadline-pressure scenario to reason through, comparing options on date, cost, and risk, adds the most to this objective and no listed mission covers schedule what-if analysis directly.

lessons.plain: Sometimes a team decides to add extra steps to a project plan to lower the chance that a known problem will hurt the work. This lesson is about how those steps get written into the official plan. The team does not just quietly add them. The change goes through a formal review, the approved change is recorded, and if the change is large enough, the team resets the reference plan that progress is measured against. That reset reference is called a new baseline. Think of it like changing the rules of a race after it has started: you can do it, but the change must be agreed, written down, and dated so everyone knows which rules applied when.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team has learned of a risk that could delay testing by three weeks, and they want to add a mitigation task to their plan. Should they simply insert the task into the schedule and keep measuring progress against the original plan, or is there a reason to do something more formal? Give your first instinct and why.
lessons.teach:
A schedule baseline is the approved version of the project schedule, saved as a reference point. Later progress is compared against it to see whether work is early, late, or on track. A performance measurement baseline, or PMB, is the broader reference: the approved schedule together with the time-phased budget for each piece of work, against which earned value (the value of work actually completed) is measured. A risk-mitigation activity is extra work added to lower the chance or impact of a known risk, such as booking a vendor readiness check. A change control process is the formal route a proposed change follows: it is submitted, assessed for its effect on time, cost and scope, approved or rejected by a designated group, and recorded.

Why it works: the baseline only means something if it changes rarely and for recorded reasons. If mitigation work slips into the plan without review, the team can no longer tell whether a delay came from the original work or from its own additions, and earned value figures become misleading.

Worked example. The PMB says integration testing finishes in week 12. Risk review approves a two-week vendor readiness check that needs budget and moves the finish. Step 1: the change request describes the new activities, their cost, and the impact on the critical path (the longest chain of dependent tasks, which sets the finish date). Step 2: the change board approves it. Step 3: the approved activities are added to the schedule model and the change is logged with a reference number. Step 4: because the approved scope and cost changed materially, the PMB is re-established as a new baseline, and the old baseline is kept for history. Step 5: future variance is measured against the new PMB.

Common mistake: adding mitigation tasks to the live schedule and still reporting variance against the old baseline. Every later report then looks like the team fell behind, when the plan simply changed.

Consequence: dashboards show false overruns, and decision makers act on figures that mix two different plans.

questions.prompt: A school district is migrating its network. The team wants a three-day vendor penetration test added as a risk-mitigation activity. Their change request says the test costs 6,000 in added budget and moves the finish date by three days because it sits on the critical path. Step 1: the change request describes the new activity, its cost, and its critical path impact. Step 2: the change board approves it. Step 3: the approved activity is added to the schedule model and the change is logged as CR-088. Step 4: [missing]. Step 5: variance for the rest of the project is measured against the new reference.
choices: Delete the old baseline so the team has only one reference and avoids confusion
Leave the PMB alone and wait until project closeout before re-baselining
Re-establish a new PMB reflecting the approved scope and cost, and keep the old baseline for history
Keep the original PMB and report variance against it, since only the critical path changed
questions.why: A material change to approved scope and cost means the PMB is re-established as a new baseline, and the old baseline is kept so history is not lost.

questions.prompt: Which description best defines a performance measurement baseline (PMB) as used in this course?
choices: A single dated milestone that marks when the project must finish
The approved schedule together with the time-phased budget for each piece of work, used as the reference for earned value
A ranked list of risks by their likelihood and impact on the project
The record of every change request submitted during the project, whether approved or not
questions.why: The PMB is the approved schedule combined with the time-phased budget, against which earned value is measured.

questions.prompt: A team adds an approved four-day vendor check to the live schedule of a payroll upgrade, but its status report still compares work against the schedule as it stood before approval. What is the most likely result?
choices: The report will likely show the team as late, even though the plan itself changed
The report will show the four-day addition as earned value, so variance is zero
The report will automatically re-baseline the project once the vendor check begins
The report is accurate because the old baseline always reflects the current plan
questions.why: Measuring against the old baseline makes the added work look like overrun, which is the false-overrun failure the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: A change request for a new data-cleansing activity is rejected by the change board. What should happen to the schedule model and the PMB?
choices: The activity is not added to the schedule model, the PMB is unchanged, and the rejection is recorded
The PMB is re-established so the rejected work is still tracked
The activity is added to the schedule model and the PMB is updated, with the rejection noted only in email
The activity is added to the schedule model but kept out of the PMB
questions.why: Only approved changes go into the live schedule and trigger PMB changes, and a rejection is still recorded through the formal process.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never run a formal change process why approved risk-mitigation work must go through change control and sometimes leads to a new PMB. Name one limit or tradeoff of resetting the baseline.
lessons.modelAnswer: Mitigation work is real work that changes the plan, so it has to be reviewed like any other change. The change request shows the added activities, their cost, and how they affect the critical path and the finish date. An approving group decides whether to accept it. Once approved, the change goes into the schedule model and is logged, so anyone can trace why the plan differs from the original. If the scope or cost change is large, we re-establish the PMB as a new baseline and keep the old one for history. The tradeoff is that resetting the baseline hides some past slippage: the new baseline looks cleaner, so reviewers must compare it with the original to see the real performance history. Resetting too often also weakens the baseline as a yardstick, so it should be reserved for material, approved changes.
rubricPoints: Mitigation work that changes scope, cost or dates must go through formal change control, not a silent edit.
Approved changes are recorded with a reference, and the impact on the critical path is shown.
A new PMB is established when the change is material, and the old baseline is kept for comparison.
Resetting the baseline can hide past slippage or weaken it as a measure if done too often.

suggested.rationale: Deciding between a simple schedule update and a formal rebaseline is a judgement call best practised through a scenario, and no listed mission covers schedule change control.

lessons.plain: A schedule is a plan of tasks with planned start and finish dates. Once work begins, the plan has to keep up with reality: tasks finish early or late, new work appears, and sometimes the whole plan must change. Updating the schedule model means recording what actually happened so the plan stays accurate. Documenting baseline changes means that when the agreed reference plan itself must move, the change is requested, reviewed by the people allowed to approve it, recorded, and kept as history. Think of a road trip: you note delays on your map every day, but you only redraw the official route through a formal decision that everyone can see.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project's finish date slips by three weeks because a supplier delivers late. Should the project manager simply type the new dates into the schedule, or does something else need to happen first? Explain your reasoning.
lessons.teach:
The schedule model is the working network of activities, durations, dependencies, and calendars that the project uses to forecast dates. The baseline is the approved reference version of that schedule, the one the team and sponsor agreed to measure performance against. Actuals are the recorded real start and finish dates and the remaining work on each activity. A variance is the gap between the baseline and the current forecast. Updating the model means entering actuals and remaining durations so the forecast is honest. Rebaselining means replacing the reference itself, which is a formal change because it changes what success is measured against. A change request is the written proposal for that change, and a change control board (CCB) is the group with authority to approve or reject it.

Worked example: activity 'Install sensors' was planned for 10 days from day 20 to day 30. On day 26 the supplier is late, so 4 days of work remain and the forecast finish is day 34. Step 1: enter the actual start and remaining duration into the model. The forecast moves four days, and the successor 'Calibrate' shifts with it. Step 2: the project finish moves from the approved day 60 to day 64, so the baseline is breached. Step 3: submit a change request with the impact on time, cost, and risk. The CCB approves, the baseline is rebaselined, and the reason and approver are logged.

Common mistake: overwriting baseline dates to match the new forecast. The original promise disappears, and variance reports then show no slip. In a running project this hides the delay from the sponsor and from contract milestones, so funding and commitments are judged on false dates.

A schedule update records what happened, while a baseline change is an approved decision that alters the agreed reference.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's warehouse racking install was planned for 6 days, from day 40 to day 46, with the project finish approved at day 90. On day 43 the crew has finished 3 days of work, but a rework issue means 5 days of work still remain, so the forecast finish is day 48. Step 1: enter the actual start on day 40 and the remaining duration of 5 days into the schedule model, which moves the forecast finish to day 48 and the successor 'Commission racks' with it. Step 2: the project finish forecast moves from day 90 to day 92, so the baseline is breached. Step 3: what is the correct next control action?
choices: Overwrite the baseline dates with the day 48 forecast so the variance report shows no slip.
Leave the model as it is and wait for the next monthly status meeting before raising anything.
Submit a change request describing the impact on time, cost and risk, and keep the approved baseline unchanged until the change control board decides.
Rebaseline immediately because the crew lead and the project manager both agree the new date is realistic.
questions.why: A breach of an approved baseline requires a formal change request reviewed by the change control board, and the reference stays fixed until that approval is given.

questions.prompt: In schedule control, what is the difference between a schedule update and a baseline change?
choices: A schedule update records actuals and remaining work in the working model, while a baseline change is an approved decision that replaces the agreed reference.
Both are the same action, and the only difference is whether the sponsor was copied on the file.
A baseline change is made by the team alone, while a schedule update needs approval from the change control board.
A schedule update is an approved decision that alters the agreed reference, while a baseline change only records what happened.
questions.why: An update records what happened in the model, whereas a baseline change replaces the approved reference and needs formal approval.

questions.prompt: A hospital IT team's approved baseline finishes its electronic records rollout on day 120. The latest update shows a forecast finish of day 126 because a server delivery slipped. The sponsor asks the scheduler to make the baseline match the forecast so the project looks on track. What should the scheduler do?
choices: Change the baseline finish to day 126 and note the reason in the status report.
Ask the sponsor to sign a memo accepting day 126 and leave the schedule model unchanged.
Delete the successor activities so the forecast finish returns to day 120.
Enter the actuals and remaining durations so the forecast is accurate, then submit a change request with the time, cost and risk impact to the change control board.
questions.why: The forecast should be updated honestly, and because the approved finish is breached, the change must go through a formal request that the change control board approves or rejects.

questions.prompt: A film studio's post-production schedule has an approved final delivery date. The team has been overwriting the baseline dates each week with the current forecast. A financier later asks why the variance report has shown zero slip for months. What is the most accurate explanation of what went wrong?
choices: The financier should have checked the calendars, because calendar errors are the usual cause of zero variance.
The team entered actuals too often, which made the variance calculation unreliable.
The change control board approved too many changes, so the sponsor lost track of them.
The variance report compares the baseline to the forecast, so overwriting the baseline with the forecast makes the gap disappear and hides the delay from the financier.
questions.why: Overwriting the baseline removes the original promise, so the variance between reference and forecast becomes zero even though the delivery date has slipped.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to scheduling why the project manager can update the schedule with actual progress without approval, but must go through formal change control to rebaseline. Name one limit or tradeoff of the formal process.
lessons.modelAnswer: Updating the schedule with actuals is a record of facts: what started, what finished, and how much work remains. That keeps the forecast honest and does not change what the project agreed to deliver, so it sits within the project manager's normal authority. Rebaselining is different because the baseline is the agreed measure of success. If we change it, we change the yardstick, so the change needs a written request with its impact on time, cost, and risk, and approval from the people who own the commitment, and it needs to be logged with the reason. The tradeoff is speed: the formal process takes time, so a small slip may wait for review while work continues. Teams that rebaseline too readily lose the ability to see real performance, so the control exists to keep that visible.
rubricPoints: Separates recording actuals and forecasts from changing the approved baseline
Explains that a baseline is the agreed reference used to measure performance
Notes that baseline changes need a change request, impact analysis, and approval
Names a tradeoff such as slower response or the risk of hiding slippage through frequent rebaselining

suggested.rationale: The core skill is articulating when a schedule update becomes a formal baseline change, which is best practiced by explaining it back rather than by a listed mission.

lessons.plain: Schedule closeout means two things at the end of a project. First, you make sure every task on the plan is either truly finished, with a real finish date recorded, or formally dropped with a reason, so nothing is left hanging. Second, you compare what actually happened with the original plan, called the baseline. The baseline is a saved copy of the schedule as it was agreed at the start. Comparing the two shows how far the project drifted, in days and in money, and gives the next team honest numbers to plan from.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project was planned to finish in 10 weeks but actually finished in 12. Before any teaching, what would you check first to find out which tasks caused the delay, and why would a saved copy of the original plan matter for that check?
lessons.teach:
A baseline is the approved schedule saved at a fixed point, usually at the start, with planned start and finish dates and a planned cost for each activity. Planned Value (PV) is the budgeted cost of the work scheduled to be done by a given status date. Earned Value (EV) is the budgeted cost of the work actually completed by that same date. Schedule Variance (SV) is EV minus PV; a negative number means the project is behind plan. Schedule Performance Index (SPI) is EV divided by PV; below 1 means behind, above 1 means ahead.

Why it works: both measures use the same budget yardstick, so planned work and completed work can be compared fairly even when tasks differ in size. Closeout adds a final check. Every activity needs an actual finish date or a documented reason it was removed, and the finish date of the whole project is compared with the baseline finish date.

Worked example: the baseline is 10 weeks with a 100,000 total budget, and 60,000 was scheduled to be done by week 6. At week 6 the team has completed work budgeted at 45,000. So PV is 60,000 and EV is 45,000. SV equals 45,000 minus 60,000, which is minus 15,000. SPI equals 45,000 divided by 60,000, which is 0.75, so the project is about 25 percent behind on scheduled work. The project then finishes in week 12. Finish variance equals 12 minus 10, which is plus 2 weeks. At the end all planned work is complete, so SV reads zero; the lateness appears in the finish-date comparison, which is why closeout compares dates directly.

Common mistake: marking leftover activities complete without recording an actual finish date, or deleting them. That erases the evidence of what slipped and when.

Consequence: if actual dates are not recorded and the baseline is overwritten, the next project's estimates have no real data behind them, and the same delay tends to repeat.

questions.prompt: A warehouse inventory software rollout has an approved baseline (the fixed schedule and budget saved at the start) of 8 weeks and a total budget of 80,000. At the week 4 status date, Planned Value (PV, the budgeted cost of work scheduled by that date) is 50,000 and Earned Value (EV, the budgeted cost of work actually completed by that date) is 40,000. Step 1: Schedule Variance (SV) equals EV minus PV, which is 40,000 minus 50,000, so SV is minus 10,000 and the project is behind on scheduled work. Step 2: Schedule Performance Index (SPI) equals EV divided by PV, which is 40,000 divided by 50,000, so SPI is 0.8. Step 3 is missing: state what the SPI of 0.8 tells the team, in plain terms.
choices: The project is 20 percent behind scheduled work, since 0.8 is below 1
The project is 80 percent complete, so 20 percent of the work remains
The SV of minus 10,000 is zero, so the schedule is on track
The project is 20 percent ahead of plan, since 0.8 is close to the 1.0 target
questions.why: An SPI below 1 means EV is less than PV, so the team has completed about 80 percent of the work it had scheduled, which is 20 percent behind plan.

questions.prompt: At a status date, a team's Planned Value (PV, budgeted cost of work scheduled to be done by then) is 70,000 and its Earned Value (EV, budgeted cost of work actually completed by then) is 77,000. Which pair of statements is correct?
choices: SV is minus 7,000 and the project is behind plan
SV is zero because all scheduled work will eventually be done
SV is plus 7,000 and the project is behind plan
SV is plus 7,000 and the project is ahead of plan
questions.why: SV equals EV minus PV, which is 77,000 minus 70,000 equals plus 7,000, and a positive SV means the project is ahead of plan.

questions.prompt: A team closes its last open activities by setting their percent complete to 100 with no actual finish date, then deletes the six activities that were postponed past the original plan. What is the main consequence for the organisation?
choices: The record of which work slipped and when is lost, so later estimates have no real data behind them
The baseline is automatically updated, so the SPI will read higher on the next project
Nothing changes, because deleted activities no longer affect the project finish date
The schedule becomes shorter, so future projects can be planned more aggressively
questions.why: Without actual finish dates or documented removal reasons, the evidence of what slipped and when disappears, so the next project's estimates cannot learn from real performance.

questions.prompt: A project's baseline finish date is 25 March. At closeout, the final Schedule Variance is zero because all planned work has been earned, but the actual finish date is 9 April. Which closeout check reveals the lateness?
choices: Trust the final SV of zero as proof the project was on time
Compare actual finish with baseline finish: 15 days late
Check the final SPI, which should read 1.0 and show on time
Compare total spend with the baseline budget only
questions.why: Closeout compares the actual project finish with the baseline finish directly, because a final SV of zero hides lateness, and 25 March to 9 April is 15 days late.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a project that closed on its last planned day can still have finished late against the original plan, and name one limit of using SPI to judge schedule health.
lessons.modelAnswer: A project can close on its final day and still be late, because the schedule to judge against is the baseline saved at the start. The fair test is the real finish date compared with the baseline finish date. Closing on a new date only shows the team's own sense of done, not whether the original plan was realistic. Schedule Performance Index is earned value divided by planned value at a status date. It is useful mid-project to see whether work is keeping pace with plan. Its limit is that it weights progress by cost, so one expensive late task can distort the reading. At closeout it also tends to read 1.0 because all planned work is done, so it stops telling you much. For that reason I would record actual finish dates against baseline dates and treat SPI as a mid-project signal rather than the final verdict.
rubricPoints: Late finish is measured against the saved baseline finish date, not against the team's own sense of done.
SPI is earned value divided by planned value at a status date and shows pace relative to plan.
Closeout requires an actual finish date or a documented removal reason for every activity.
SPI has limits, such as cost weighting that can distort the picture and a reading near 1.0 at the end.

suggested.rationale: Working through a mid-project status calculation and a closeout finish comparison together builds both the arithmetic and the judgment this objective needs.

lessons.plain: When a project finishes, the people who lived through it know what went well and what hurt. Soliciting stakeholder feedback means asking the people who depended on the schedule, or were affected by it, what they noticed: which dates slipped, which handoffs were late, which assumptions turned out false. Those observations become lessons learned, which are short records of what happened, why, and what to do differently. Turning them into scheduling best practices means changing how the next schedule is built so the same mistake does not come back. Think of it like a post-game review where coaches, players, and referees each speak, and the notes end up in the playbook.
lessons.guessPrompt: A six-month office fit-out finished two weeks late, and the project team says the delay was just bad luck. Before you read on, what would you ask the people outside the project team to learn whether the delay was luck or a pattern that could repeat?
lessons.teach:
A stakeholder is anyone affected by the schedule or able to affect it, such as a client, a supplier, a regulator, or a team that waits on your work. Feedback is their account of what helped and what hurt. A lesson learned is a short, specific record that links an event to its cause and to a response, for example: approval took three weeks because the permit office needs a full drawing set, so submit drawings earlier. A best practice is a lesson that has been checked against more than one project and written into how schedules are built. Why it works: the project team sees its own work from the inside and tends to blame outside factors or forget small delays. Stakeholders see the handoffs, so they notice what the team missed.

Worked example: a fit-out project ends two weeks late. Step one, ask each stakeholder the same questions: where did you wait, where were you surprised, what did you need earlier. Step two, the electrical contractor says inspection slots were booked out for three weeks, which the schedule never showed. Step three, the schedule data confirms the inspection activity had a one-day duration and no calendar constraint. Step four, record the lesson as cause, effect and trigger, then turn it into a practice: book external inspection slots at planning time and add a lead-time check to the planning template.

Common mistake: gathering feedback only from the project team, or writing lessons as vague wishes such as communicate better. Consequence: a lesson without a cause and a practice is never reused, so the next project repeats the same three-week wait.

questions.prompt: A software team in a hospital pharmacy rolls out a new dispensing system and finishes four days late. Step one: the team asks each stakeholder the same three questions about where they waited, where they were surprised, and what they needed earlier. Step two: the pharmacy technician lead says the staff training rooms were fully booked for two weeks, which the schedule never showed. Step three: the schedule data shows the training activity lasted one day with no room constraint. Step four is missing: the team has written the lesson as a cause (room bookings were not planned), an effect (training slipped two weeks), and a trigger (the room was not reserved at planning). Which step completes the lesson by turning it into a practice?
choices: Ask the technician lead to rewrite the training plan for the next rollout
Book training rooms at planning time and add a room lead-time check to the planning template
Drop the lesson, since one late rollout is not enough evidence to act on
Survey only the pharmacy software team again to confirm the training delay
questions.why: The practice turns the recorded cause into a planning step that prevents the repeat, which is the step the teaching text requires after the cause, effect and trigger are recorded.

questions.prompt: Which statement best separates a lesson learned from a best practice in schedule closeout?
choices: Any stakeholder comment that is rated as very important by the project sponsor during the review meeting
A lesson learned and a best practice are the same record, differing only in how long the write-up is
A lesson checked across several projects and written into how schedules are built
A one-off note about a single event that the team records for its own file, with no link to any cause
questions.why: The teaching text defines a best practice as a lesson that has been checked against more than one project and written into how schedules are built, while a lesson learned is a single linked record of event, cause and response.

questions.prompt: A closeout review for a warehouse relocation collected feedback only from the internal scheduling team and recorded the outcome as communicate better. Which two problems does this review have?
choices: It should have written a cost variance instead of a lesson, since cost is easier to measure
It gathered feedback from one group only, and the lesson has no cause or practice attached to it
It asked too many stakeholders, and the lesson is too detailed to reuse on later projects
It should have waited until the relocation was finished before asking anyone for any input
questions.why: The teaching text names both failures: feedback gathered only from the project team, and lessons written as vague wishes that have no cause and no practice, so they cannot be reused.

questions.prompt: A regulator's sign-off on a clinic extension took four weeks because the application lacked an environmental report. The schedule showed the sign-off as a two-day activity with no lead time. Which lesson record follows the format the teaching text describes?
choices: Regulators are slow, so future projects should simply allow more buffer time before any sign-off is due.
Cause: missing report. Effect: four-week sign-off. Trigger: report not checked at planning. Practice: add a documents-and-lead-time check to the planning template.
Cause: the project manager was too busy. Effect: four-week delay. Trigger: the schedule was too long. Practice: hire more staff for the next clinic project.
The sign-off was late because the applicant team did not work fast enough, so next time the project manager should push harder and ask the regulator for faster service on every single application.
questions.why: The correct record links the event to its cause, effect and trigger and then to a practice that prevents the repeat, which is the structure the teaching text gives for a usable lesson.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has just joined the project why we ask stakeholders for feedback at closeout instead of only reviewing our own team's notes, and name one limit of stakeholder feedback we should keep in mind.
lessons.modelAnswer: We ask stakeholders because they see the handoffs and waits that our team cannot see from inside, such as an approval queue or a supplier's lead time, and they often remember delays we treated as normal. Their feedback is only the start, though. Each comment has to be checked against schedule data, because people sometimes blame the wrong cause, or describe a problem that was really caused by a late change request. The limit is that stakeholders have their own interests, so a supplier may stress outside factors and downplay its own delays. So we record each lesson as cause, effect and proposed practice, test it against the schedule, and only then adopt it as a best practice for future planning.
rubricPoints: Stakeholders see handoffs and waits that the project team cannot see from inside
Feedback must be checked against schedule data before it is trusted
Stakeholders have their own interests, which can bias what they report
A lesson is recorded with cause, effect and a proposed practice, then adopted as a best practice only after testing

suggested.rationale: Explaining feedback-driven lessons back to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it.

lessons.plain: After a project finishes, the team has learned things that would save time next time: which estimates were too optimistic, which supplier delivered late, which scheduling setting caused confusion. Updating organizational process assets means writing those lessons into a shared, findable place, such as a company library of past-project records and templates, so the next team starts with them instead of rediscovering them. A lesson kept only in one person's head or inbox does not count as an update.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project team finished and agreed that its testing estimates were too optimistic. Six months later a new team plans a similar project. Where should that lesson have been written so the new team would find it, and why would a private chat message to the old team not be enough?
lessons.teach:
Organizational process assets are the reusable things an organization keeps for running projects. They include standard templates, process guidelines, estimating guides, and historical records of past work. A lessons learned entry is a written record, drawn from a finished project, of what happened, why it happened, and what a future team should do differently. Documented means the entry is written in a form that someone who was not on the project can find and understand without asking the author. Updating the assets means adding or revising these entries in the shared store.

This matters because schedules are built from history. When a new team estimates a task, it leans on how long similar tasks actually took. A recorded lesson changes those future numbers. Without it, each team repeats the same planning errors.

Worked example. A project's integration testing was planned for 5 days but took 14. Step 1: state the facts, planned 5 days and actual 14 days. Step 2: find the cause, which was a shared test environment that another team had booked. Step 3: state the recommendation, which is to reserve a dedicated environment or add a buffer for shared resources. Step 4: write the entry with the project name, date, category, impact, cause, and recommendation. Step 5: file it in the shared repository and update the estimating guide's duration history for integration testing.

Common mistake: writing vague notes such as 'testing was hard', or leaving the entry in one project folder. Neither helps a future team plan.

Consequence: if the entry is missing, the next planning template still shows the 5-day assumption, so the new baseline repeats the same slip.

An update counts only when the next project can find the entry and use it.

questions.prompt: A payroll-reporting project planned 3 days for reconciling source data but took 9 days. The team's entry is partly written. Step 1, state the facts: planned 3 days, actual 9 days. Step 2, find the cause: the source files arrived in an unexpected format and needed manual cleaning. Step 3, state the recommendation: run a format check at kickoff and add a buffer for data cleaning. Step 4 is done: the entry is written with project name, date, category, impact, cause and recommendation. Step 5, the one remaining action, is not yet taken. What is it?
choices: Save the entry in the shared repository where future estimators can find it, and revise the duration history for data reconciliation
Wait until the next annual audit before recording anything
Delete the project folder to free storage space
Email the sponsor a summary and close the project file
questions.why: An update only counts when a future team can find the entry and use it, so the entry must go into the shared store and the estimating history must be revised.

questions.prompt: In the context of organizational process assets, what does it mean for a lessons learned entry to be documented?
choices: The author has signed the entry and stored a copy in personal notes
The entry is long enough to fill at least one full page of a template
The entry is written so that someone who was not on the project can find and understand it without asking the author
The entry lists every person who worked on the project
questions.why: Documented means the entry is written in a findable, understandable form for outsiders, which is the definition given in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: A team's lesson reads: 'The supplier was late, so we should be more careful next time.' Which change would make this a usable lesson learned entry?
choices: Rename the file with the current year so it sorts correctly
Shorten the note to one sentence so it is easier to read
Add the supplier's full company address and phone number
Add the planned and actual durations, the specific cause of the delay, and a concrete recommendation such as adding buffer for supplier deliveries
questions.why: The teaching text says vague notes do not help planning, and a usable entry states facts, cause and recommendation, which the correct choice adds.

questions.prompt: A team recorded a lesson learned from a finished project but left it only in that project's folder. A new project then used the planning template, which still assumed the old duration. What is the consequence?
choices: The new project finishes early because the template is more accurate than before
The original project's budget is automatically reduced by the difference
Nothing changes, since the template is always rebuilt from scratch by the estimator
The new baseline repeats the same planning slip, because the update did not count without a findable entry in the shared store
questions.why: The teaching text states that a missing or unshared entry leaves the old assumption in the template, so the new baseline repeats the error.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what it means to update organizational process assets with documented lessons learned. Name one limit or tradeoff of keeping a lessons-learned repository, such as the effort of writing entries or the risk that old lessons stop fitting new situations.
lessons.modelAnswer: Organizational process assets are the reusable knowledge a company keeps for running projects: templates, process guidelines, and historical records. When we close a schedule, updating them means writing the lessons we learned into the shared repository in a form someone else can use. The entry records the planned value, the actual result, the cause, and a recommendation. For example, if integration testing ran three times longer than planned because of a shared environment, the entry records that cause, and the estimating guidance is revised to reflect it.
