The main tradeoff is effort and quality. Entries take time to write, and a repository full of vague or outdated notes becomes hard to search, so people stop trusting it. Entries should be reviewed and tagged by topic and context so a future team can judge whether a lesson still applies to its own situation.
rubricPoints: Defines organizational process assets as reusable company knowledge such as templates, guidelines, and historical records.
Explains that the lesson must be written in a shared, findable place rather than kept only in memory.
Describes what a useful entry contains: planned versus actual, cause, and recommendation.
Names a limit or tradeoff, such as writing effort or lessons that no longer fit new contexts.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the idea to a teammate, including its limits, is the core skill, and no listed mission or planned engine covers it.

lessons.plain: When a project finishes, the people who paid for it, approved it, or depend on its dates need to know how it really went. A final schedule report is the summary that says what was planned, what actually happened, and how far apart those two things are. One part of that report uses a small set of comparisons called earned value, which put schedule and money side by side. Distributing the report means choosing who receives it, in what form, and making sure they can read the numbers without a guide. Think of it like the final scorecard after a season: the scores matter, but so does a short note explaining why the team fell short of its plan.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project was planned to finish $100,000 of work by month six. By month six it has completed work that was budgeted at $80,000, and it has spent $90,000 to do that work. Before reading on, do you think the project is ahead of, behind, or on plan for its schedule, and is it over or under budget for the work it has finished?
lessons.teach:
Earned value management, or EVM, measures schedule and cost together using three figures. Planned value (PV) is the budgeted value of the work you scheduled to finish by a given date. Earned value (EV) is the budgeted value of the work actually completed. Actual cost (AC) is the money really spent to complete that work. Two variances follow. Schedule variance (SV) equals EV minus PV, and a negative number means the project is behind. Cost variance (CV) equals EV minus AC, and a negative number means the project has spent more than the completed work was worth. Two indices scale these as ratios. The schedule performance index (SPI) is EV divided by PV, and the cost performance index (CPI) is EV divided by AC. Below 1.0 is unfavorable for both. The method works because it compares like with like: raw spending alone cannot show whether a project is healthy, since spending can look high simply because more work is done.

Worked example: at month six, PV is 100,000, EV is 80,000 and AC is 90,000. Step one, SV is 80,000 minus 100,000, which is minus 20,000. Step two, CV is 80,000 minus 90,000, which is minus 10,000. Step three, SPI is 80,000 divided by 100,000, which is 0.80. Step four, CPI is 80,000 divided by 90,000, about 0.89. Both indices are below 1, so the report should state that the project is behind schedule and over cost for the work completed.

A common mistake is publishing variance figures without the baseline they were measured against. The baseline is the original approved plan, and a stakeholder cannot judge a number without knowing which plan it compares to. The final report must name the baseline and the date of measurement. In closeout, this matters because archived figures later feed contract disputes and lessons learned, and a number stripped of its basis can mislead the next project.

questions.prompt: A warehouse fit-out is reported at month four with PV 240,000, EV 216,000 and AC 198,000. Step one: SV is 216,000 minus 240,000, which is minus 24,000. Step two: CV is 216,000 minus 198,000, which is plus 18,000. Step three, the schedule performance index (SPI, EV divided by PV), is missing. Step four: the cost performance index (CPI, EV divided by AC) is about 1.09. What is the missing SPI?
questions.why: SPI is EV divided by PV, so 216,000 divided by 240,000 gives 0.90, below 1.0 and consistent with the negative schedule variance.

questions.prompt: A subcontractor's cost variance on a clinic renovation is +6,000 at the report date. Which reading is correct?
choices: The cost performance index is above 1.0, so the project is over cost
The completed work was worth 6,000 more than the money spent to finish it
The project has spent 6,000 more than the completed work was worth
The project is 6,000 behind the scheduled value of work
questions.why: A positive cost variance means EV exceeds AC, so the completed work is worth more than what was spent on it.

questions.prompt: A county road resurfacing has PV 500,000, EV 430,000 and AC 410,000 at the report date. Which pair of indices is correct?
choices: SPI 0.86, CPI 1.05
SPI 0.86, CPI 0.95
SPI 1.16, CPI 0.95
SPI 0.80, CPI 1.05
questions.why: SPI is 430,000 divided by 500,000, or 0.86, and CPI is 430,000 divided by 410,000, or about 1.05.

questions.prompt: A software vendor reports PV 900,000, EV 1,000,000 and AC 1,200,000 for a completed module. Which statement belongs in the final report?
choices: Ahead of schedule and over cost for the work completed
Behind schedule and over cost
On schedule and under cost
Behind schedule and under cost
questions.why: Schedule variance is +100,000 (ahead) and cost variance is -200,000 (more spent than the completed work was worth).

lessons.explainPrompt: A sponsor asks for a one-page summary of how the project finished against plan. In your own words, explain to a teammate which EVM figures you would include, what a negative cost variance and a schedule performance index below 1 each tell the sponsor, and one limit of these numbers that you would state in the report.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would include the final planned value, earned value and actual cost, plus schedule and cost variance and their indices, all tied to the approved baseline and the measurement date. A negative cost variance means we spent more than the completed work was budgeted to cost, so the sponsor should expect the budget to have been overrun for what was delivered. A schedule performance index below 1 means we earned less work than we had planned by that point, so the project finished later than baseline. The limit I would state is that these figures reflect only the work the plan defined and how it was measured; if the scope changed, or if the work was recorded at inconsistent points, the indices can look better or worse than reality. I would say that plainly so nobody reads the numbers as a complete verdict.
rubricPoints: Names the EVM inputs (PV, EV, AC) and what each measures
Explains what a negative variance or an index below 1 signals
States that figures must be tied to the named baseline and date
Gives at least one limitation of the numbers for the audience

suggested.rationale: Choosing and explaining EVM figures to a non-specialist audience is the core skill here, and no listed mission has the learner do that.

lessons.plain: Archiving schedule files means making a sealed, labeled copy of the documents that describe how a project's timeline was built, how it was managed, how it progressed, and every change made to it, then storing that copy so it can be found and read years later. People need this for two reasons: a contract may require the project to keep records for a set time, and if the project is later disputed, someone must reconstruct what happened and when. Think of it like keeping the logbook of a voyage. The final map alone does not tell you where the ship turned or why.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project finished three months late and the customer is asking why. Would the final version of the schedule file alone be enough to explain the delay? Say what you would also want to keep.
lessons.teach:
An archive is a frozen, labeled copy of project records, stored in a controlled place so it can be retrieved and read later. For schedule closeout, the archive normally holds four kinds of record. The schedule model is the working file itself: the activities, durations, dependencies, resource assignments and calendars, saved in a form that can be reopened. The schedule management plan is the written set of rules for how the schedule was built, updated and controlled. Status reports are the periodic records of progress and forecast dates. The change log is the record of each requested schedule change, its decision and its reason. Baselines, the approved snapshots of the schedule used as the reference point for measuring performance, should be kept as separate dated versions.

Why this works: a finished schedule shows only the end state. Forensic analysis, meaning reconstructing the sequence of events to explain why a result happened, needs the history. Contracts often require records to be kept for a fixed period, so the archive also serves as evidence of what was agreed.

Worked example: a contractor claims a six-week delay caused by the owner in month five. Step one: open the baseline version approved before month five. Step two: open the change log and list the entries dated in that window. Step three: compare the status reports for the same months to see when the forecast end date moved and which activities consumed float. Step four: match each change to its approver. The result shows whether the slip came from an approved owner change or from contractor performance.

Common mistake: archiving only the final file and deleting older versions to save space. Without the baseline and change log, the team cannot show what was agreed or when, so a defensible position can be lost in a dispute.

questions.prompt: A warehouse automation project's client says a conveyor installation was moved later without approval. An archivist works through it in order. Step one: open the baseline saved before the installation window opened. Step two: open the archived schedule model dated the month the move first appears and read the installation activity's start date. Step three is missing. Step four: check the change log for an approved entry that covers the difference. Which action fills step three?
choices: Compare the installation activity's start date and float in the baseline with the same activity in the archived model dated that month, to find the size and timing of the difference.
Save a new baseline over the old one so its dates match the current model.
Delete the older status reports, since the latest model already shows the current dates.
Ask the equipment vendor to rebuild the baseline from memory of the dates agreed at kickoff.
questions.why: Comparing the two dated versions shows exactly what moved and when, which must be known before the change log can be checked for an approval.

questions.prompt: In schedule closeout, why are baselines kept as separate dated versions instead of being overwritten each time the schedule is updated?
choices: So the agreed reference point can be compared with any later state, even after the working file has changed.
So the change log is no longer needed once a baseline exists.
So the working file stays small enough to open quickly on shared drives.
So only the most recent version counts as the contractual record.
questions.why: A dated baseline preserves the approved reference point so later performance and changes can be measured against what was agreed at the time.

questions.prompt: A school building project has closed out. Eight months in, the finish date moved, and the owner now disputes who caused it. Which archived record is most useful for finding out whether an approved change explains the move?
choices: The schedule management plan, because it lists the rules for building the schedule.
The change log entries dated around month eight, each matched to its approver and reason.
The lessons-learned summary written after the project ended.
The final schedule model, because it shows the finish date that was reached.
questions.why: The change log records each requested change with its decision, reason and date, which allows the timing and approval of a shift to be tested directly.

questions.prompt: A hospital wing's project is closed, and the team deletes its older baselines and status reports to free storage. The contract requires records to be kept for seven years. What is the main consequence?
choices: The team cannot show the agreed reference dates or the reasons for past changes, which weakens its position if a dispute arises.
The contract becomes void because the records no longer match the final model.
The final schedule model stops being readable once the older versions are removed.
There is no consequence, because the end-state file already contains the full project history.
questions.why: Without baselines and the change history, the team cannot demonstrate what was agreed or when, and a contractual retention requirement is breached.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we only need to archive the final schedule file once the project closes, since it already shows the finished dates. Explain to them what else belongs in the archive, why each item matters, and one limit of what an archive can prove.
lessons.modelAnswer: The final file shows where the project ended, but not how it got there. The archive also needs the baseline versions, which are the approved reference snapshots, so we can compare planned against actual. It needs the change log, which records each change request, who approved it and why, so we can tell owner-driven slips from contractor-driven ones. It needs the status reports, which show when forecast dates moved over time, and the schedule management plan, which shows the rules we followed. Together these let someone rebuild the sequence of events and check our claims. One limit: an archive proves what was recorded at the time, not what was intended. If status reports were filled in late or inaccurately, the archive will faithfully preserve weak evidence, so we should note how and when each record was created.
rubricPoints: Names the baseline versions as the reference needed to compare planned against actual
Explains that the change log with approvals is needed to attribute delays
Notes that status reports and the management plan show how dates moved and which rules applied
States a limit, such as an archive preserving only what was recorded and possibly inaccurate records

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly a set of artifacts and retention requirements, which a written explanation covers better than any current OpsForge mission or planned engine.

lessons.plain: Stakeholders are the people who care about how a project turns out: the sponsor who funds it, team members who build it, customers who use the result, and managers who depend on its dates. Developing and fostering relationships with them means building enough trust over time that they hear bad news early, ask useful questions, and respond quickly when a decision is needed. A communication management plan is the agreed written guide that sets out who needs which information, how often, in what format, and who to contact when something goes wrong. Relationship work is what makes that plan actually work, because a plan that exists only on paper tends to be ignored the moment the schedule slips.
lessons.guessPrompt: A sponsor has been receiving a short weekly status email for two months. This week the schedule has slipped by a week, and the sponsor has not heard about it yet. Should you wait for the regular Friday email, or contact the sponsor now, and what would make your choice reasonable?
lessons.teach:
A stakeholder is anyone whose interests can be affected by a project or who can affect it. A communication management plan is the agreed document that defines what information each stakeholder receives, how often, through which channel, and how escalation works when a problem appears. Developing and fostering stakeholder relationships means the ongoing work of building trust so that the plan is followed in practice and the people in it respond well. It works because people act on information they believe. When a sponsor knows the scheduler will report slips promptly and accurately, the sponsor can make decisions in time and does not need to dig for the truth.

Worked example. A vendor delivery is late and the critical milestone slips six days. The plan says the sponsor receives a one-line weekly summary, and any slip over five days triggers a direct note within one working day. Step one: check the plan and confirm the six-day slip crosses the threshold. Step two: send the sponsor a short note the same day with what slipped, the new date, and the impact on the next milestone. Step three: state the one decision needed, such as approving overtime or accepting a later date. Step four: log the message and confirm the follow-up time in the plan.

A common mistake is treating the relationship as separate from the plan. Some schedulers are pleasant in informal chats but then hold back bad news until the weekly report, which breaks the plan's trigger and damages trust. Others send long reports that nobody reads, so the important point is lost.

In a running project, the consequence is clear. If the sponsor hears about a slip from another team before hearing from the scheduler, the sponsor loses confidence and starts asking for daily reports, which adds overhead for everyone involved.

questions.prompt: A regional logistics firm is installing new warehouse scanner firmware. The communication plan says the operations manager receives a direct phone call within one working day for any slip over four days. The install slipped eleven days. Step one: the scheduler checked the plan and confirmed eleven days crosses the four-day threshold, so a direct call is required. Step three: the scheduler identified the one decision needed, which is whether to approve a weekend crew or accept a later go-live. Step two is missing. Which action completes step two?
choices: Call the operations manager the same day using the channel the plan names, giving the new install date and the impact on go-live
Ask the firmware vendor to inform the operations manager directly so the scheduler does not have to make the call
Hold the news until the Friday weekly summary so the update is complete before anyone is contacted
Send the operations manager a full twelve-page variance analysis covering every task in the project
questions.why: The plan requires a direct message through its named channel, sent promptly with the new date and milestone impact, which is the missing step two the scenario needs.

questions.prompt: In a communication management plan, which description best fits the document itself?
choices: A record of every risk the team has identified since the project began
A personal list of tasks the scheduler plans to finish each week
A contract that sets the payment terms with each vendor on the project
An agreed document defining what each stakeholder receives, how often, through which channel, and how escalation works
questions.why: The teaching text defines the plan as the agreed document covering information content, frequency, channel, and escalation for each stakeholder.

questions.prompt: A city transit project's sponsor has asked for prompt news of any problem. The plan says the sponsor gets a one-line weekly summary, and a direct note is required only for a slip over five days. A ticketing task has slipped three days this week. What should the scheduler do?
choices: Send a direct note to the sponsor today, because the sponsor asked to hear about problems promptly
Hold the three-day slip for the weekly summary, since the plan's direct-note trigger is not crossed
Schedule a call with the sponsor to discuss the three-day slip and agree on how often to report
Copy the sponsor on every task update each day so nothing can be missed
questions.why: Because the three-day slip is below the five-day threshold, the plan's weekly one-line summary is the correct channel, so the scheduler follows the plan rather than sending a direct note.

questions.prompt: A scheduler is friendly and open in informal chats with the sponsor, but a seven-day slip on a critical milestone is held until the next weekly report. What is the most likely consequence for the running project?
choices: The weekly report becomes shorter because the slip is removed from the summary
The project moves faster because the team no longer spends time on direct notes
The sponsor approves a schedule extension immediately because the news arrives in a formal document
The sponsor's trust in the plan is damaged, the trigger is broken, and the sponsor may begin asking for daily reports
questions.why: The teaching text says holding back bad news breaks the plan's trigger and damages trust, and that the sponsor then asks for more frequent reports, adding overhead.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a new teammate how building stakeholder relationships connects to the communication management plan, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on relationships to guide communication.
lessons.modelAnswer: The communication management plan says who needs what information, how often, and when to escalate. Relationships are what make people actually use that plan. If a sponsor trusts that I will report slips promptly, they respond to my notes quickly, and the plan's triggers work. I would tell the new teammate to follow the plan's cadence and thresholds even when the relationship feels good, because a friendly chat does not replace a formal escalation. One limit is that relationships are personal and can change when people leave or priorities shift, so the plan is what keeps communication consistent when a contact changes. A tradeoff is time: building trust takes regular, small interactions, and that effort competes with producing the schedule itself. I would protect a few minutes each week for stakeholder contact and log what was discussed so the next person can pick it up.
rubricPoints: Explains that the communication management plan defines who receives what, how often, and the escalation triggers
Explains that relationships and trust make stakeholders act on the information the plan delivers
Names a concrete limit or tradeoff, such as personal relationships changing or time cost
Shows that the plan is followed even when informal contact is good

suggested.rationale: Explaining how relationships and the communication plan work together is the core skill here, and no listed mission or planned engine practises it directly.

lessons.plain: Schedule visibility means that the people who need to know where a project's timeline stands can see it, and that what they see is current and accurate. It is not a one-off report. The project manager needs a detailed, up-to-date view to make decisions, and stakeholders need a simpler, regular picture that shows whether key dates are holding. Think of a station departure board: it only helps if someone updates it when a train is late, and if each person waiting can read the information that matters to them.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project finish date was agreed three months ago, but nobody has looked at the schedule since. On Monday a sponsor asks whether that date still holds. What is the main problem, and what would you put in place so this does not happen again?
lessons.teach:
Schedule visibility is the condition in which the current schedule, the approved baseline, and actual progress are available to the right people, at the right frequency, in a form they can read. The baseline is the approved version of the schedule, and it is the reference point for measuring progress. Variance is the difference between a planned date and the actual or forecast date. Total float is how far a task can slip before it pushes out the project finish. A look-ahead is a short window, such as the next two to four weeks, showing detailed upcoming work. The communication management plan is the agreed record of who receives which schedule information, how often, and in what format.

It works because decisions depend on current facts. A stale schedule creates false confidence, and people plan around dates that the team already knows are wrong.

Worked example. The baseline finish is 30 June. At week 12, the design sign-off task was planned to finish 10 May but actually finished 17 May, a slip of 7 days. That task has 3 days of total float. Step 1: record the actual date against the baseline. Step 2: find the variance, 7 days. Step 3: subtract the float, leaving 4 days that flow into the successor tasks. Step 4: forecast the new finish as 4 July. The project manager sees the detail, and the sponsor receives a short update with the new forecast and the decision needed.

Common mistake: publishing the schedule file without entering actual dates, so the visible schedule still shows the project on time.

Consequence: stakeholders keep planning around 30 June, and the gap appears late, which damages trust in the schedule and in the project manager.

questions.prompt: A warehouse fit-out team planned its floor anchor task to finish on 12 February. It actually finished on 17 February. The task has 8 days of total float, and the baseline finish is 2 April. Step 1: record 17 February as the actual finish against the baseline. Step 2: the variance is 5 days. Step 3: compare the 5-day variance with the 8 days of float, which leaves 0 days flowing into successor tasks. Step 4 is missing. What is the correct forecast for the project finish, and what does it mean for the sponsor update?
choices: The finish stays at 2 April because the slip is absorbed by float, so the sponsor needs no forecast change, though the project manager still sees the task-level variance.
The baseline is reset to 17 February so the variance reads zero, and the sponsor is told the schedule is on time.
The finish moves to 7 April by adding the full 5-day variance to the baseline, so the sponsor is told to expect a delay.
The finish moves to 30 March because the float was used up, so the sponsor gets an update with that date.
questions.why: Because the 5-day slip is smaller than the 8 days of float, no successor is pushed out, so the finish forecast stays at 2 April while the detailed variance still goes to the project manager.

questions.prompt: A task has 6 days of total float. Which statement describes what that float means?
choices: The number of extra days the team has booked for the task in the calendar.
The number of days between the planned start and the actual start of the task.
The number of days the task can slip before the project finish date moves.
The gap between the baseline finish and the current forecast of the whole project.
questions.why: Total float is defined as how far a task can slip before it pushes out the project finish, so the correct choice describes that limit directly.

questions.prompt: A city road resurfacing team publishes a weekly schedule file. The progress percentages are updated, but no actual finish dates are entered, so the variance column shows zero for every task and the status looks on time. What is the most likely cause of the misleading view, and what should the team do before the next release?
choices: The file was not updated with actual dates, so variance cannot show the slip; the team should enter the actual dates and reissue the schedule before stakeholders read it.
The sponsor should be told to ignore variance until closeout, because variance is not useful during execution.
The baseline was set incorrectly, so the team should re-baseline the project to the current dates this week.
Total float is too large on the non-critical tasks, so the team should remove float to make the schedule tighter.
questions.why: Variance is measured from actual dates, so leaving them out hides slips; entering actuals and reissuing before release prevents stakeholders from planning around stale dates.

questions.prompt: A software rollout task slips 10 days, which uses up all of its total float and pushes the project finish 4 days past the baseline. Which communication step best fits the situation according to the schedule visibility approach?
choices: Tell the sponsor only that the team is working on the delay, without giving a date.
Give the sponsor a short update with the new forecast finish and the decision needed, and give the project manager the detailed task-level variance.
Send the full schedule file to every stakeholder on the same day so they can see the change for themselves.
Wait for the next monthly status report so the change is reported alongside other updates.
questions.why: The approach matches the detail to the audience: the project manager gets the full variance, while the sponsor gets a short forecast-and-decision update.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has just joined the project how you would keep the project manager and stakeholders able to see the schedule accurately. Name one limit or tradeoff in how often you update them.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would keep one baseline and one live schedule, and I would enter actual dates every week, before the status meeting, so the view is never stale. The project manager gets the detailed schedule and look-ahead. Stakeholders get a shorter summary, agreed in the communication management plan, showing the key milestones, the current forecast, any variance, and any decision they need to make. The main tradeoff is frequency. Weekly updates keep the picture current but cost time and can create noise over small movements, while monthly updates are cheaper but can hide a slip until it is hard to recover. I would set the cadence to match how fast the schedule changes and how much the stakeholders can act on, and I would revisit it if the project's risk changes.
rubricPoints: Visibility requires actual dates to be updated on a regular cadence, not just a schedule file being shared
The project manager and stakeholders receive different levels of detail, as agreed in the communication management plan
Variance against the baseline and the effect on the finish date, considering float, should be shown
Update frequency involves a tradeoff between currency and effort or noise

suggested.rationale: Reasoning through a schedule status scenario about who needs what update and when adds more than reading alone, and no listed mission covers project scheduling communication.

lessons.plain: When a project is running, the people paying for it or depending on it need to know two things: is the schedule on track, and if it is not, what are we doing about it and what does that change for them? This objective is about writing or saying that news clearly to senior managers and other stakeholders. A good update is short, states the facts behind the status, names the fix you are applying, and spells out the effect of that fix on the dates the audience cares about. Think of it like a weather forecast with a plan attached: here is where we are, here is what we will do, and here is when we now expect to arrive.
lessons.guessPrompt: A project was due to finish on 1 June. Halfway through, the team has fallen about two weeks behind, and a fix would add some cost but could save the date. Before reading on, write the two or three things you think a senior sponsor most needs to hear in one short message.
lessons.teach:
Start with the baseline: the agreed original plan with its planned dates. The forecast finish is the end date you now expect, based on what has actually happened and what remains. The variance is the gap between them, usually counted in working days. The critical path is the chain of dependent tasks that sets the earliest possible finish; a delay on it moves the end date, while a delay on a task with float (also called slack, the room a task can slip without moving the end date) usually does not. A corrective action is a change you make to bring work back toward the plan, such as adding people, changing sequence, or reducing scope. Its impact is the change it causes to dates, cost, scope, or risk.

Worked example. Baseline finish is 1 June. A network installation task on the critical path is ten working days late, so the forecast is about 15 June. Step one: state the baseline and the forecast together. Step two: state the variance, which is roughly two weeks, and name the critical-path cause. Step three: state the corrective action, which is adding a second crew for five days that recovers four days. Step four: recalculate the forecast to 11 June. Step five: state the cost, an extra 8,000 credits, and the risk that the second crew may introduce rework. Step six: state the decision you need from the sponsor, whether to approve the spend.

Common mistake: reporting activity effort ('the team is 70 percent busy and working hard') without the date impact, or burying a forecast slip under cheerful wording. Consequence in a running system: the sponsor approves plans and books vendors against the old date, so a hidden slip turns into a missed handover and extra charges later.

A status update that does not state the new forecast and the decision needed is incomplete.

questions.prompt: A regional college's archive scanning project has a baseline finish of 20 October. The scanning task sits on the critical path and is 8 working days late, so the forecast finish is 3 November (a Monday). Step one, stating the baseline and forecast together, and step two, stating the variance of about two weeks with the critical-path cause, are done. Step three: the corrective action is a second scanner operator for 4 days, which recovers 3 working days. Step four is missing. Step five: the extra cost is 2,500 credits, with the risk that the new operator needs training time. Step six: the decision needed is sponsor approval of the spend. What is the missing step four?
choices: Keep the forecast at 3 November, since the second operator is only a corrective action and does not change dates.
Keep the original variance and report the forecast as 15 November.
Add the 3 recovered days to the forecast, giving 6 November.
Recalculate the forecast to 29 October, three working days earlier than 3 November.
questions.why: The corrective action recovers 3 working days from the 3 November forecast, so the recalculated forecast is 29 October, and the other options either ignore the recovery or add days in the wrong direction.

questions.prompt: A warehouse fit-out project has a baseline finish of 5 May. A painting task has 6 working days of float and is now 4 working days late, with no other changes to the plan. Which status statement is correct?
choices: The forecast finish stays at 5 May, and the painting task has used 4 of its 6 days of float, which remaining buffer should be reported.
The forecast finish stays at 5 May and no float has been used, so there is nothing to report.
The painting task is now on the critical path and the project is 4 days late.
The forecast finish moves to 9 May because the painting task slipped.
questions.why: A delay on a task with float usually does not move the end date, but the float consumed should still be reported so the sponsor sees how much buffer remains.

questions.prompt: A status email for a data migration with a baseline finish of 14 March says: The team is 85 percent busy and morale is high, so we are doing well. What is the main failure in this update?
choices: It is written in a casual tone and should use a formal greeting.
It covers too few tasks, so the sponsor cannot see every workstream.
It reports effort without a new forecast finish or the decision needed from the sponsor.
It is missing the sponsor's signature, so it is not valid.
questions.why: An update that describes team activity without the date impact, the forecast finish, or the decision needed is incomplete and can hide a slip.

questions.prompt: A corrective action for a software release adds two testers for 6 working days at a cost of 3,000 credits and recovers 5 working days. Which item is an impact of the corrective action rather than the action itself?
choices: Moving the testing task earlier in the sequence of work.
The 3,000 credit cost and the risk that the new testers miss defects.
Adding two testers for 6 working days.
The baseline finish date agreed at the start of the project.
questions.why: Impact is the change a corrective action causes to dates, cost, scope, or risk, so the added cost and the new risk are impacts while the testers and the sequence change are the actions themselves.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has just joined the project what a schedule status update to senior management must contain when a corrective action is proposed, and name one limit or tradeoff of the fix you are recommending.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would tell the sponsor three things. First, the baseline finish and the current forecast, with the variance between them in working days. Second, the cause, which is the late task on the critical path, because delays elsewhere may be absorbed by float. Third, the corrective action and its impact: what we will do, the new forecast, the extra cost, and any new risk it creates. Then I would ask for the specific decision we need, such as approving the spend by a named date. The tradeoff I would name is that the second crew only recovers part of the slip and adds coordination effort, so the new forecast is an estimate, not a guarantee. I would say that openly, with the range of likely outcomes, so the sponsor does not treat it as a firm commitment.
rubricPoints: States the baseline and current forecast together with the variance
Identifies the critical-path cause rather than general effort
Describes the corrective action and its impact on dates, cost, or risk
Names a specific decision or approval needed from the audience
Acknowledges a limit or tradeoff, such as uncertainty in the new forecast

suggested.rationale: Explaining the update and its tradeoffs back in your own words is the core skill, and no listed mission practises stakeholder messaging.

lessons.plain: When a project's timeline is at risk, the people who depend on it need to hear about it early, in a form they can act on. This objective is about spotting schedule problems that could also change what the project delivers (its scope) or break the rules the team agreed for managing the schedule (the schedule management plan), then telling the right people. Think of a rail operator who learns a bridge is closed. They do not wait for the next timetable review. They tell the depot, the passengers and the freight partner, each with the detail that matters to them. The skill is choosing who needs to know, what they need to know, and whether the problem is big enough to go up a level.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team finds that a supplier delivery slipping two weeks would force you to drop a feature the customer asked for. Before reading on, who needs to hear about this, and what should they hear first?
lessons.teach:
Start with the terms. A schedule baseline is the approved set of planned dates the project is measured against. A scope baseline is the approved description of what the project will deliver. The schedule management plan is the agreed set of rules for how the schedule is built, tracked and changed, including what size of date change needs formal approval. A stakeholder is anyone affected by the project or able to affect it. The communication management plan records who receives which information, how often, and through which channel. Escalation means raising an issue to someone with the authority to decide, such as the sponsor.

Why it works: a schedule problem is rarely only about dates. When a delay threatens a finish date or forces a scope trade-off, the people who own those commitments need to know while options still exist. Telling them early, in the right form, keeps decisions with the people who hold them.

Worked example. A supplier says a key component will arrive two weeks late. Step 1: confirm the impact on the critical path, which shows the finish date moves two weeks. Step 2: compare with the schedule baseline; the committed date is missed. Step 3: check scope; the feature that needs the component cannot be finished before the deadline. Step 4: check the schedule management plan, which says any finish-date change above five days needs sponsor approval through change control. Step 5: send the sponsor an escalation stating the impact, the two options, and the decision needed by a set date. Send the customer contact the scope impact in the form the communication plan specifies, and update the team's task dates.

Common mistake: holding the news for the next routine status meeting, or sending every stakeholder the same detailed report. Consequence: when a scope cut or date change surfaces late, approvals are bypassed and the baseline changes without agreement, so reported progress no longer means what stakeholders think. Good communication here means the right person hears the right impact, with a decision attached, before the options are gone.

questions.prompt: A county library renovation has a finish date that is now at risk. Step 1: the electrical contractor reports that the permit inspection will slip six days, so the reopening date moves six days on the critical path, meaning the chain of tasks that sets the earliest finish date (the critical path). Step 2: the reopening date in the schedule baseline, the approved set of planned dates, is missed. Step 3: the lighting upgrade cannot be completed before reopening, so the scope baseline, the approved description of what will be delivered, is affected. Step 4 is missing. Step 5: the library director, who owns the reopening commitment, receives an escalation (a message raising the issue to the person with authority to decide) stating the impact, two options, and a decision date. Which missing Step 4 fits the scenario? Note that the schedule management plan sets the rules, including the size of date change that needs formal approval through change control, which is the formal approval process for changes.
choices: Hold the news for the next routine monthly meeting so the director gets one consolidated update.
Update the schedule baseline to the new reopening date so that status reports show the project on track.
Send the same detailed inspection report to all twelve stakeholders so that nobody can claim they were not informed.
Check the schedule management plan, which says any finish-date change above three days needs formal approval, so the approver is identified before the escalation is sent.
questions.why: Step 4 is where the learner checks the schedule management plan's approval threshold, which determines who must decide before any change is recorded.

questions.prompt: Which document records the agreed rules for how the schedule is built, tracked and changed, including the size of date change that needs formal approval?
choices: The schedule baseline, which holds the approved planned dates.
The schedule management plan, which sets the rules for building, tracking and changing the schedule.
The communication management plan, which records who receives which information and how often.
The scope baseline, which describes what the project will deliver.
questions.why: The schedule management plan is defined in the teaching text as the set of rules for schedule building, tracking and change, including approval thresholds.

questions.prompt: A team lead quietly moves a milestone date inside the project's tracking tool so that the next status report shows no slip, without raising it with anyone. What is the most likely consequence, according to the unit's reasoning?
choices: The scope baseline is updated to match the new date, which is the required fix.
The stakeholders gain earlier warning, because the date change is visible in the tool.
Reported progress no longer matches what stakeholders believe, and the baseline changes without agreement or approval.
The sponsor is automatically alerted by the communication management plan, so no harm is done.
questions.why: The teaching text warns that when changes surface late or are made without approval, the baseline changes without agreement and reported progress stops meaning what stakeholders think.

questions.prompt: A finish-date forecast slips by four days. The schedule management plan requires sponsor approval only for finish-date changes above five days, and the slip does not force any scope trade-off. What is the appropriate next step?
choices: Update the team's task dates and pass the status change to stakeholders through the channel and frequency the communication management plan specifies.
Hold the update until the next routine status meeting so that all stakeholders hear it together.
Escalate to the sponsor for formal approval, since any slip at all must go through change control.
Send the full detailed report to every stakeholder on the list, since a consistent message is always best.
questions.why: Below the plan's five-day threshold, no sponsor approval is needed, so the right response is to update tasks and inform stakeholders through the planned channel and frequency.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who has never run a schedule how you decide whether a slipping task should be escalated to the sponsor or simply handled within the team. Name one limit or tradeoff of escalating too early or too late.
lessons.modelAnswer: I check two things first: whether the slip changes a baseline or the scope, and whether the schedule management plan says a change of that size needs approval. If the critical path moves, or the planned finish date or a committed scope item is affected, I escalate to the sponsor, because only they can accept the new date or trim scope. If the slip is absorbed by float and nothing committed moves, I keep it within the team and record it in the status report. The tradeoff is that escalating too early creates noise and can make stakeholders stop trusting the signal, while escalating too late removes the options that would have been cheap. So I escalate with a clear impact, a few options, and a decision date, not just a warning.
rubricPoints: Identify whether the issue changes the schedule baseline, the scope, or a rule in the schedule management plan
Name the stakeholder who holds the authority to decide and escalate to them
Tailor the message to each stakeholder group as the communication plan specifies
Include impact, options and a decision needed by a date, not just a warning
Name a tradeoff of escalating too early (noise) or too late (lost options)

suggested.rationale: Choosing who to tell and what to tell them is best practised by reasoning through a realistic slip scenario, which this objective calls for.

scenarios.title: Northgate Warehouse Routing Upgrade: Setting the Schedule Approach
scenarios.scenario:
Northgate Freight Systems is a fictional mid-sized logistics software company. It has just approved a 14-month project to replace the routing engine used by three regional warehouses. You have been named the project scheduler, a role that owns the schedule model, its rules, and how it is updated. Your sponsor wants a scheduling approach in place before the team starts work next week. Three facts shape the setup. First, the company's enterprise environmental factors (EEFs, meaning conditions outside the project that still affect it, such as the tools the company already licenses and how its governance board works) include a shared corporate scheduling tool that finance and the PMO can read but that most engineers have never used. Second, the organizational process assets (OPAs, meaning the company's own internal templates, policies, and lessons from past projects) include a rule that any change to the approved finish date must be reviewed by the steering committee. Third, the software team is split between a fixed-scope integration phase, where the requirements are known, and a discovery phase where the routing rules are still being worked out with warehouse staff.

Please answer the following in your scheduling approach memo to the sponsor.

1. Describe the configuration management policy you would set for the schedule: who may view it, who may edit it, where the master copy is stored, and how a baseline (the approved snapshot of the plan that progress is measured against) is locked and how changes to it are approved.

2. Recommend the scheduling approach for each of the two phases, including the level of activity granularity (how finely work is broken into tasks), whether you would apply earned value management (EVM, a method that compares planned value, earned value, and actual cost to judge progress) and at what level, and which tool you would use for each phase and why.

3. Explain how you will communicate the scheduler's role and the scheduling procedures to the team, so that the engineers who have not used the corporate tool know what they are expected to do.
subParts: Configuration management policy for the master schedule and baseline
Scheduling approach per phase: granularity, EVM use, and tool choice
Communicating the scheduler role and procedures to the team
modelAnswer: Set the master schedule in one controlled file on the shared corporate tool, stored in a single location with version history turned on. Give the PMO and finance read-only access, give the project team view access, and limit edit rights to the scheduler and one named backup. Lock the baseline once the sponsor and steering committee approve it, so the approved dates cannot be overwritten. Any change to the approved finish date goes to the steering committee, as the company's OPA rule requires, and any change inside the float (the spare time before a task delays the finish) can be approved by the scheduler and logged. Keep a change log that records who asked, why, the impact on the finish date, and the approval date, so the baseline can always be compared with the current plan.

For the fixed-scope integration phase, use a detailed, predictive plan: break work into tasks of roughly one to two weeks each, with clear dependencies (links showing which task must finish before the next starts). Apply EVM at the work package level so cost and schedule performance are measured against a locked baseline. Use the corporate tool because it is already the company standard and finance reads it. For the discovery phase, plan in short time-boxed iterations (fixed-length work periods, such as two weeks) with coarser tasks, and track progress by completed iterations rather than detailed EVM, since the scope will change. Use a lighter team board tool for the day-to-day discovery backlog and push summary dates into the corporate schedule so the two views stay consistent. Justify both choices by the level of uncertainty in each phase.

Hold a short onboarding session in which you explain three things: the scheduler owns the master file and the baseline; team members update their own task status by a fixed weekly deadline and do not edit dates or links; and any date that threatens the approved finish must be raised to the scheduler the same day. Give each engineer a one-page guide with screenshots showing how to update status, how to flag a blocked task, and how to request a change. Run a dry-run update in week one, check that every task has an owner and a status, and review the process at the end of the first month, adjusting the procedure where people are still confused.

scenarios.title: Brightwater Modular Labs: Sensor Rig Delivery Schedule
scenarios.scenario: Brightwater Modular Labs is a fictional company that builds calibration rigs for a customer. The contract's statement of work (SOW, the document listing what must be delivered and when) requires the finished rig to be delivered by day 12 of the project. You are the new project scheduler and have been given a small network of activities. The critical path is the longest chain of dependent activities through the network; it sets the earliest possible finish date. Float (also called slack) is how many days an activity can slip without delaying the finish. The activities are: A Design (3 days, no predecessors); B Procure parts (5 days, no predecessors); C Fabricate frame (4 days, must follow A); D Assemble (2 days, must follow both B and C); E Test and ship (3 days, must follow D). Use the forward pass (earliest start and finish, working left to right) and backward pass (latest start and finish, working right to left from the deadline) to answer the following. 1. Identify the critical path, the total project duration, and the float on activity B. 2. The fabrication supplier gives a three-point estimate for C: optimistic 3 days, most likely 4 days, pessimistic 9 days. Use the PERT weighted average (a three-point method that gives weight to the most likely value, computed as (optimistic + 4 times most likely + pessimistic) divided by 6) to recompute C, and state whether the day-12 milestone still holds. 3. A Monte Carlo simulation (running the schedule thousands of times with random durations drawn from each activity's range) shows only a 35 percent chance of finishing by day 12. The steering group's risk tolerance (the confidence level it will accept before committing to a date) is 80 percent. Explain what the result means and propose one decision you would take to the steering group.
subParts: Critical path, total duration and float on B
Recomputed duration of C using the PERT average and milestone check
Interpretation of the Monte Carlo result and a proposed decision
modelAnswer: The forward pass gives A finishing at day 3, B at day 5, C at day 7 (it starts after A), D starting at day 7 because it waits for the later of B and C, finishing at day 9, and E finishing at day 12. The backward pass from the day-12 deadline gives E latest start 9, D latest start 7, C latest start 3, A latest start 0, and B latest finish 7 so latest start 2. The critical path is A, C, D, E: the chain with zero float, which sets the 12-day total. Activity B has 2 days of float (latest start 2 minus earliest start 0), so it can slip 2 days without delaying the finish. A common mistake is treating the longest-duration activity as critical; B is the longest single activity at 5 days yet is not critical, because the path is about the chain of dependencies, not single durations. Consequence: any slip on A, C, D or E pushes the day-12 delivery.

PERT weighted average for C = (3 + 4 times 4 + 9) divided by 6 = (3 + 16 + 9) divided by 6 = 28 divided by 6, about 4.67 days, up from the 4-day estimate. Since C is on the critical path, the path length becomes 3 + 4.67 + 2 + 3 = 12.67 days, which is about 0.67 days past the day-12 milestone. The milestone does not hold under the revised estimate with the current sequence. The answer must show the calculation and the conclusion; stating only the average is incomplete.

The Monte Carlo result means that, with the activity ranges as entered, the schedule finishes by day 12 in only about 35 of every 100 simulated runs. The steering group wants 80 percent confidence, so the current plan does not meet its risk tolerance. The point is not that the average finish is wrong; it is that the spread of outcomes puts the milestone at high risk. A reasonable proposed decision is to take a specific, testable action rather than just reporting the number: for example, ask the fabrication supplier to commit to a firm 4-day lead time or pay for expedited shop time on C, which shortens the critical path, then rerun the simulation to see whether the probability reaches the 80 percent target. Alternatively, the group could agree to negotiate a later delivery date with the customer. Either way, the steering group decides; the scheduler presents the evidence and the options, and should record the decision and the revised baseline.

scenarios.title: Conveyor Controller Slip at Hollis Freight Tooling
scenarios.scenario:
Hollis Freight Tooling Ltd is a fictional company that builds warehouse sorting software. You are the scheduler for its Northgate release, which must reach a go-live readiness milestone on day 120 of the project calendar. The schedule model is the working plan with dates, durations, and links between activities. The performance measurement baseline (PMB) is the approved version of the plan, including scope, schedule, and cost, against which progress is measured; once approved, it changes only through formal change control, which is the documented process for requesting, reviewing, and approving changes. Total float is the number of days an activity can slip before it delays the milestone. The critical path is the chain of activities with zero or the least total float that sets the earliest finish date.

At the week 14 status meeting, the team reports that the integration test of the conveyor controller, planned to finish on day 112 with 4 days of total float, has been delayed six working days because the vendor delivered its interface late. The test team now estimates that the remaining test effort will take eight working days after the vendor drop. Separately, the risk board approved risk response R-07, which adds a second test environment. That environment needs three working days to set up and would cut the remaining test effort from eight working days to five, but it is not yet in the schedule model. The approved baseline still shows the original dates. Your sponsor wants a recommendation on whether to keep the current plan, add R-07, or do something else, and asks you to handle the schedule update correctly so that performance reporting stays honest.

Answer the following.

1. Explain how you would record this week's status in the schedule model, and what the analysis shows about the effect on the day 120 milestone.
2. Describe a what-if scenario comparing keeping the single test environment with adding the second environment, and state which option you would recommend based on the numbers.
3. Explain what formal steps are needed before the approved R-07 mitigation can be placed into the schedule, and whether this creates a new PMB.
subParts: Record status and analyse the milestone impact
What-if comparison of the two test options
Formal change control for R-07 and PMB handling
modelAnswer: Record the actual vendor delivery and the revised remaining duration in the schedule model as status updates, without changing the approved baseline dates or the baseline itself. The model should show the test activity finishing later than its baseline finish of day 112. Its planned total float was 4 days, and the six-day delay consumes all 4 days and then pushes the milestone by 2 days, so the day 120 milestone moves to about day 122 on the current plan. Report this as a variance against the baseline: the activity is late by six working days, the float is consumed, and the milestone is forecast to slip by two days. Mention that the eight-day remaining effort is the current forecast and that the forecast drives the milestone figure, not the original estimate.

Build two scenarios from the same status-updated model. Scenario A keeps one environment: the eight remaining days run after the vendor drop, and the milestone finishes about two days late. Scenario B adds the second environment: three days of setup run first, then the remaining effort drops to five days, which can be run partly in parallel. Compare the resulting finish dates, the cost of the extra environment, and the remaining float on the milestone path. Recommend the option that restores the day 120 milestone or limits the slip to what the sponsor accepts, and note any assumptions such as whether the setup can start immediately. Keep the what-if results separate from the live plan so the baseline is not changed by the analysis.

R-07 is an approved risk response, but adding it to the schedule still changes the plan, so it must go through formal change control. Submit a change request describing the reason, the added activities, the setup and cost effects, and the impact on the milestone. The change control board reviews and approves it, and only after approval is the change placed into the schedule model. Because the approved scope, schedule, and cost change, the PMB is re-established as a new baseline, and the old baseline is kept for historical comparison. Record the change in the change log with its approval date, the reason, and the new baseline version. Do not silently edit the existing baseline or update only the dates, since that would hide the variance from the sponsor and make later performance reports misleading.

scenarios.title: Closing out the Dockside Expansion schedule
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Line Fabrication is a fictional mid-sized company that builds steel mezzanines and conveyor systems for warehouses. Its project, the Dockside Expansion, has just finished, and Priya, the project scheduler, must complete closeout. The approved schedule baseline (the frozen plan of dates and budget that actual performance is compared against) called for 120 working days and a budget at completion (BAC, the total budget for all the work) of $480,000. The project finished on day 132. Final cost records show $512,000 actually spent, which is the actual cost (AC). Because all scope was delivered, the earned value (EV, the budgeted value of work actually completed) is $480,000. Management also wants the schedule model, the management plan, the monthly status reports and the change log archived, because the client contract requires seven years of records and a delay-penalty dispute is possible. Complete the following:
1. Calculate the cost variance (CV, which is EV minus AC) and the cost performance index (CPI, which is EV divided by AC), and state what each result means for the final report.
2. Describe how Priya should gather stakeholder feedback and record lessons learned so they can be added to the organization's process assets (OPAs, the reusable templates, guidelines and historical records a company keeps for future projects).
3. List the schedule files that must be archived and explain why each one matters for a forensic review, meaning a later investigation into what happened and why.
subParts: Cost variance and CPI from final figures
Stakeholder feedback and lessons learned into OPAs
modelAnswer: CV = EV minus AC = $480,000 minus $512,000 = -$32,000. CPI = EV divided by AC = 480,000 divided by 512,000, which is about 0.94. A negative CV means the project spent more than the value of the work it delivered, and a CPI below 1.0 means each dollar spent bought about 94 cents of planned work. The final report should state that the project finished 12 days late (day 132 against the baseline of day 120) and $32,000 over the earned value, and should show the calculation so stakeholders can trace it. Priya should not report the schedule variance as a cost figure; the 12-day overrun is a time variance and must be shown separately.

Priya should hold short structured interviews or a closeout workshop with the sponsor, the client representative, the site foremen, the procurement lead and the finance analyst, asking what caused the delay, what scheduling estimates were wrong, and which practices helped. Each answer should be written as a lesson with a cause, an effect and a recommended practice, for example: the racking delivery lead time was estimated at 10 days but was 24 days, so future schedules should use the supplier's recent actual lead times. Priya then enters these lessons into the lessons-learned register and submits them to the process owner, who updates the OPAs such as the estimating template and the risk checklist, so the next project starts with the better practice. A lesson that is written down but never added to a reusable asset has not been captured.

Priya should archive the schedule model (the file with all activities, durations, logic links and resources), the schedule management plan (the document stating how the schedule is built, changed and reported), the status reports (the monthly records of actual progress and forecasts) and the change log (the record of each approved or rejected change, with its date and reason). Together they show what the baseline was, how it was changed and when, and what the team knew at each point. In a forensic review, the baseline and change log prove whether a delay was caused by the client or by the contractor, and the status reports show when a problem was first visible. Without these files, Harbor Line could not defend itself against a delay-penalty claim, because it could not prove which changes were approved. The archive should be kept in a read-only location for the contract period, with a checksum or version record so no one can later claim the files were altered.

scenarios.title: Packaging Line Slip at Harbor Lane Foods
scenarios.scenario:
Harbor Lane Foods is a fictional mid-sized food packaging company. It is installing a new packaging line at its plant in Redfern Vale, and you have just been appointed scheduler for the project. The schedule baseline (the approved original plan of dates, which every later forecast is compared against) puts commissioning, meaning the formal handover of the working line, on 14 March. Last Tuesday the equipment vendor said the control cabinet will arrive late. The critical path (the longest chain of dependent tasks, which sets the earliest possible finish for the whole project) now runs through that cabinet delivery. The forecast finish has moved 9 working days later than baseline. Total float (how long a task can slip before it pushes the finish date) on that chain was only 2 days, so the slip is well beyond the buffer. The communication management plan (the document that states who needs which information, how often, and in what format) names Dana Okafor, the operations director and project sponsor (the executive who owns the business case and funds the project), as needing a written update within 2 working days of any forecast finish change larger than 5 working days. The escalation path (the ordered list of who to inform when a decision is beyond your authority) runs from the project manager, Luis Ferreira, to the steering committee. The vendor has also said that a changed cabinet model may require the commissioning test scope, which is part of the approved scope baseline, to be revised. Answer the three sub-tasks below as the scheduler.

1. Draft the targeted written update for the sponsor. Say what changed, the new forecast finish, the corrective-action options you can see (for example, paying for expedited freight or running parallel work), and the schedule and cost impact of each option, then state the decision you need from her and by when.

2. Decide which parts of this issue must be elevated beyond the sponsor, to whom, and why. Refer to the scope and schedule management plan threshold and the possible test-scope change.

3. Set the visibility approach for the next four weeks: what you will give Luis Ferreira, what you will give the wider stakeholder group, how often, and in what form.
subParts: Draft the targeted written sponsor update: change, new forecast, corrective-action options with their impacts, and the decision needed by when.
Identify what must be elevated beyond the sponsor, to whom, and why, using the schedule management plan threshold and the scope risk.
Set the four-week schedule visibility approach for the project manager and wider stakeholders, including cadence and format.
modelAnswer: Subject: Packaging line commissioning forecast moved 9 working days. Dana, the control cabinet vendor has reported a late delivery. Baseline commissioning is 14 March; the current forecast is 26 March, a slip of 9 working days, which exceeds our 2 days of total float on the affected chain. Options: (a) expedited freight on the cabinet, which we estimate recovers 4 working days at an extra cost of about 6,000 dollars and no change to scope; (b) start the cabinet-independent wiring and panel tests in parallel, which may recover 3 working days with some rework risk and no added cost; (c) accept the 26 March date with no action. Options a and b together could bring the forecast to about 19 March. I need your decision on whether to approve option a by Thursday so the freight can be booked before the vendor's cutoff, and whether you accept the rework risk in option b. The vendor may also change the test scope, and I will confirm that within 3 working days.

Elevate beyond the sponsor to the steering committee via Luis Ferreira, the project manager, because the issue touches the scope baseline and the schedule management plan threshold. The 9-day slip is above the 5-day trigger, so it requires the written update the plan names, which goes to the sponsor. Because the possible change to the commissioning test scope alters an approved scope item, that change needs a formal change request through the escalation path to the steering committee, not a decision made in the schedule. The committee, not the scheduler, decides whether to accept a scope change or add budget for expedited freight beyond the sponsor's approval limit, if any.

Give Luis Ferreira a daily short status note on the critical path and float, plus a same-day flag for any new vendor date. Give the wider stakeholder group, including plant supervisors and the quality lead, a weekly one-page schedule update every Monday covering the forecast finish, the variance against baseline, the top two risks, and the next decision date. Use a shared dashboard or tracker so anyone can see the current forecast without asking. Hold a 30-minute review with Luis each Wednesday to check that the corrective actions are working, and send the sponsor a written update whenever the forecast moves again by more than 5 working days, in line with the communication management plan.
